Writing in Greek, he used allegorical interpretation to harmonize the Torah with Platonic and Stoic philosophy, notably in his treatises on Genesis such as On the Creation of the World. His Logos doctrine and exegetical method deeply influenced the Church Fathers, though Rabbinic Judaism largely ignored him.

Philo of Carpasia (Philo Carpasius) was a Greek-speaking bishop of Carpasia (Karpasia), a town on the Karpas Peninsula of Cyprus, active in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. He was ordained by Epiphanius of Salamis and is the first known bishop of the see. He is chiefly known for his commentary on the Song of Songs, an allegorical interpretation of the biblical book. A letter to a monk named Eucarpios and some fragments are also attributed to him.

Philostorgius (368 – c. 439) was a Greek church historian and an Anomoean, a follower of the radical Arian theology of Eunomius of Cyzicus. He was born at Borissus in Cappadocia and moved to Constantinople at about twenty. His Church History, in twelve books, appeared between about 425 and 433 and told the story of the Arian controversy from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost, but much of it survives in an epitome made by Photius in the ninth century and in passages borrowed by later writers. His treatise against Porphyry is entirely lost.

Philoxenus of Mabbug (c. 440–523), also called Xenaias, was a Syriac theologian and bishop, and one of the finest Syriac prose writers of late antiquity. Born in Beth Garmai in the Persian Empire and educated at Edessa, he became bishop of Mabbug (Hierapolis) in 485. He was a vigorous opponent of the Council of Chalcedon and a leading champion of Miaphysite Christology. He sponsored the Philoxenian revision of the Syriac New Testament and wrote thirteen Discourses on the Christian life, as well as letters and polemical treatises. Exiled under Emperor Justin I in 519, he died in exile in Thrace.

Phoebadius (also Phaebadius; French Phébade; died c. 392) was bishop of Agen in southern Gaul and a leading Western defender of Nicene orthodoxy during the Arian controversy. His surviving treatise Liber contra Arianos (c. 357–358) attacks the second creed of Sirmium, the creed its opponents called the "Blasphemy of Sirmium". At the Council of Ariminum in 359 he was among the bishops who resisted the pro-Arian party, and he took part in later councils as well. Jerome mentions him among illustrious writers. A Libellus fidei is also attributed to him, though its authorship is uncertain.

Photius (c. 815–893) was a Byzantine scholar and statesman who served twice as patriarch of Constantinople, from 858 to 867 and from 877 to 886. He was still a layman when he was appointed to replace the deposed Ignatius. His dispute with Rome produced the Photian schism, and he took a leading part in the mission to the Slavs. He was the foremost intellectual of the ninth-century revival of learning. His works include the Bibliotheca, a set of reviews of 279 books, the Amphilochia, homilies and writings against the Paulicians. The Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint.

Pierius was a Christian priest at Alexandria in the late third century. He probably led the Catechetical School there, perhaps jointly with Achillas, while Theonas was bishop. His learning as a biblical interpreter and preacher earned him the name "Origen the Younger." Some later writers call him a martyr. Jerome, however, says he survived the Diocletianic Persecution and spent his last years in Rome, where he died sometime after 309. Only fragments of his writings survive, including comments on the First Epistle to the Corinthians. He is commemorated on 4 November.

Pinytus was bishop of Knossos in Crete in the later second century, active around 170. Little is known of his life apart from what Eusebius of Caesarea reports. Eusebius counted him among the leading church writers of his time and praised his orthodoxy and his care for his flock. Dionysius of Corinth wrote to him urging him not to impose too heavy a burden of celibacy on his people. In his reply, Pinytus asked Dionysius to give them "solid food" rather than milk, meaning more advanced teaching for believers who were growing in faith. He is venerated as a saint.

Polemius Silvius was a Latin author active in southeastern Gaul in the mid-fifth century. He is known for an annotated Julian calendar from around 448–449, also called a laterculus or fasti. It tried to bring the traditional Roman festival cycle together with the newer Christian holy days. He dedicated the work to Bishop Eucherius of Lyon. Alongside the calendar it contains supplementary lists, including Roman emperors and usurpers, so it is useful evidence for late antique chronology. It also shows how pagan and Christian ways of marking time existed side by side in Gaul.

Polybius of Rhinocorura is presented as a disciple of Epiphanius of Salamis (d. 403) and as bishop of Rhinocorura, on the coast between Egypt and Palestine. He is known only from the Greek Life of Epiphanius. That work claims to be written by Epiphanius's companions John and Polybius, and Polybius is named as the author of its closing section, which recounts the saint's last days and death. Scholars generally regard the Life as a later, largely legendary composition, so whether Polybius was a real person and when the work was written remain uncertain.

Polycarp (c. 69–c. 155) was bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor and is counted, with Clement of Rome and Ignatius of Antioch, among the chief Apostolic Fathers. Irenaeus, Tertullian and Jerome report that he was a disciple of John the Apostle. His only surviving writing is the Epistle to the Philippians, which is full of echoes of the New Testament writings. Late in life he went to Rome to discuss the date of Easter with Bishop Anicetus. According to the Martyrdom of Polycarp, he was burned at the stake as a martyr in Smyrna.

Polycrates of Ephesus (fl. c. 130–196) was a bishop of Ephesus in the late second century. He led the churches of Asia Minor in the Quartodeciman controversy, defending their custom of keeping Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan. He convened a synod and wrote to Pope Victor of Rome, appealing to the tradition of the apostles Philip and John, of Polycarp, and of Melito. Fragments of the letter survive through Eusebius. In it he says that seven of his relatives had been bishops before him. The Acts of Timothy were later attributed to him, but this attribution is doubtful.

Pomponius was a Latin Christian poet, probably of the late fourth or early fifth century, though his dates and background are uncertain. He wrote the Versus ad gratiam Domini, sometimes called Tityrus, a short cento made up of lines and half-lines taken from Virgil. Modelled on Virgil's first Eclogue, it is a pastoral dialogue between the shepherds Meliboeus and Tityrus that changes Virgil's verses into a statement of Christian faith. It belongs to the late antique tradition of Christian Virgilian centos.

Pontianus was a sixth-century North African bishop whose see is not known. He was one of the Western opponents of Emperor Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters. Around 544–545, when he was asked to sign the imperial edict, he wrote a letter to Justinian that survives. In it he urged the emperor to withdraw the anathemas against Theodore of Mopsuestia and the other writings involved. He said he had not read the condemned works and that judging the dead belongs to God. He also warned that the condemnation would weaken the authority of the Council of Chalcedon.

Pontius the Deacon (died mid-third century) was a Latin Christian writer from Carthage and a deacon under Bishop Cyprian of Carthage. He stayed with Cyprian through his exile and up to his martyrdom in 258. Soon afterwards he wrote the Vita Cypriani (Life and Passion of Cyprian), which is generally regarded as the earliest Christian biography in Latin. It praises Cyprian's conversion, his time as bishop and his death, and Jerome later named Pontius as its author. Pontius is honoured as a saint. The separate proconsular acts of Cyprian's martyrdom are usually treated as anonymous.

Adeodatus I, also called Deusdedit or Deodatus (died 8 November 618), was bishop of Rome from 615 until his death. He was a Roman priest, and the first priest elected pope since John II in 533. Tradition credits him with the first use of lead seals, or bullae, on papal documents. Very few writings survive under his name. They include a letter addressed to Gordianus, a bishop of Seville, whose authenticity is doubtful. He is venerated as a saint, with a feast day on 8 November.

Anastasius I was bishop of Rome from 27 November 399 until his death on 19 December 401. He was a Roman, the son of Maximus, and succeeded Siricius. His pontificate is remembered mainly for his part in the Origenist controversy. After Rufinus translated Origen's writings into Latin, Anastasius condemned them. In a surviving letter to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, he discusses Rufinus. He also urged the North African bishops to resist Donatism. Jerome praised his holiness, and he counted Augustine and Paulinus of Nola among his friends. He was buried in the Catacomb of Pontian.

Benedict I (Latin Benedictus I) was bishop of Rome from 2 June 575 until his death on 30 July 579. His pontificate came at a hard time for Byzantine Italy, as the Lombards were expanding across the peninsula and Rome was suffering from famine. Little is known of his activity as pope. A few letters are attributed to him, including a fragment addressed to the patriarch of Grado and a letter to a bishop named David, but their authenticity is uncertain. Pelagius II succeeded him.

Boniface I was bishop of Rome from 28 December 418 until his death on 4 September 422. Supporters of the rival claimant Eulalius disputed his election, and Emperor Honorius finally settled the dispute in Boniface's favour. As pope he worked to maintain church discipline and defended Roman jurisdiction over Illyricum. He restored the rights of the metropolitan sees of Narbonne and Vienne, freeing them from the primacy of Arles. A contemporary of Augustine of Hippo, he received dedications of some of Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings. His letters and decrees survive.

Boniface II, of Germanic (Gothic) descent and born in Rome, was the first Germanic bishop of Rome. He reigned from 22 September 530 until his death on 17 October 532. His predecessor Felix IV had designated him as successor. A majority of the Roman clergy elected a rival, Dioscorus, instead, but the schism ended when Dioscorus died a few weeks later. Boniface tried to name the deacon Vigilius as his own successor, then withdrew the decree. In a letter to Caesarius of Arles, he confirmed the Second Council of Orange (529) and its teaching on grace against Semi-Pelagianism.

Boniface IV was bishop of Rome from 608 until his death on 8 May 615. He had served as a deacon under Gregory the Great and, like him, ran the Lateran Palace as a monastery and encouraged monasticism. With the emperor Phocas's permission he converted the Pantheon into a church. In 610 he held a synod in Rome attended by Bishop Mellitus of London, which addressed the needs of the young English Church. Letters to King Æthelberht of Kent are associated with this synod. He is venerated as a saint.

Boniface V was bishop of Rome from 23 December 619 until his death on 25 October 625. He is remembered for supporting the Christianisation of Anglo-Saxon England, and for a decree that made churches places of sanctuary. Bede's Ecclesiastical History preserves several of his letters. They include one to Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, which sent him the pallium, and others to King Edwin of Northumbria and his Christian queen Æthelburh, urging Edwin to convert.

Caius, also called Gaius, was bishop of Rome from 283 until his death in 296. Little reliable information about him survives. The Liber Pontificalis, which draws on the legendary acts of Susanna of Rome, makes him a Dalmatian and a relative of Diocletian. It says he decreed that clergy must pass through the lower orders before becoming bishop. Legend also holds that he baptized converts, hid in the catacombs and died a martyr, though his death came before the Great Persecution. A single decree preserved under his name is generally considered spurious.

Celestine I (Latin Caelestinus; c. 359–432) was bishop of Rome from 422 until his death in 432. He spent much of his pontificate opposing teachings judged heretical. When Cyril of Alexandria appealed to him about Nestorius, Celestine authorised Cyril to condemn Nestorius if he did not recant, and this led to the Council of Ephesus in 431. He supported the Gallic bishops' mission of Germanus of Auxerre to Britain against Pelagianism in 429. He also sent Palladius as bishop to the Christians of Ireland. Some writings that circulated under his name are not his own.

Cornelius was bishop of Rome from March 251 until his death in June 253. During his short pontificate he faced a schism led by the rigorist presbyter Novatian, who refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed under persecution. Backed by Cyprian of Carthage, Cornelius held that the lapsed could be restored after penance. A Roman synod confirmed his election and excommunicated Novatian. His surviving letters, including correspondence with Cyprian, record the controversy. Exiled under Trebonianus Gallus, he died in banishment and is venerated as a martyr.

Damasus I (c. 305–384) was bishop of Rome from 366 until his death. His election was contested, and rival factions fought violently over it. As pope he opposed Arianism, Apollinarianism and Macedonianism, and he worked to repair relations with the Church of Antioch. He was Jerome's patron and encouraged the Latin revision of the Bible that became the Vulgate. He promoted the veneration of the Roman martyrs, restored their tombs and composed verse epigrams for them, which were carved in stone by Furius Dionysius Filocalus. Letters attributed to him also survive.

Dionysius was bishop of Rome from 259 until his death in 268. His pontificate began just as Valerian's persecution gave way to the toleration granted by Gallienus, and he reorganised the Roman church after the persecution. Christians from the Libyan Pentapolis complained to him about anti-Sabellian statements made by Dionysius of Alexandria, and he held a Roman synod in response. His only surviving writing is a letter against the Sabellians, preserved in part in Athanasius's De Decretis. It rejects both Sabellianism and any division of the Godhead, and it denies that the Son is a created being.

Eusebius was bishop of Rome for a few months, from April to August 309 or 310, during the unrest that followed the Diocletianic persecution. The Roman church was then divided over how to treat Christians who had lapsed under persecution. Eusebius insisted they do penance before being readmitted, and a faction led by Heraclius opposed him. The emperor Maxentius exiled both leaders, and Eusebius died in Sicily. An epitaph by Pope Damasus records these events. No genuine writings by him survive. Letters attributed to him, such as those in the Pseudo-Isidorean Decretals, are later forgeries.

Eutychian (Eutychianus) was bishop of Rome in the late third century. The Liber Pontificalis dates his reign from 275 to his death in 283, but Eusebius gives him only ten months, so its length is uncertain. Almost nothing reliable is known about him, though his original epitaph was found in the catacomb of Callixtus. Later tradition says he allowed the blessing of produce such as grapes and beans at the altar and buried many martyrs himself. Decrees and an exhortation to presbyters attributed to him are later forgeries, associated with the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. His feast is kept on 8 December.

Felix I was bishop of Rome from 269 until his death on 30 December 274. He was born in Rome and succeeded Dionysius. His pontificate came during the controversy over Paul of Samosata, the deposed bishop of Antioch, whose removal was finally enforced through Emperor Aurelian. Tradition credits Felix with a dogmatic letter on the unity of Christ's person, and a fragment of it was cited at the Council of Ephesus. Modern scholars widely consider that fragment an Apollinarian forgery, and the decretals later attributed to him are spurious. He was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus.

Felix III, sometimes numbered Felix II because his predecessor of that name is often counted as an antipope, was bishop of Rome from March 483 until his death on 1 March 492. A Roman cleric of aristocratic family, he is traditionally regarded as an ancestor of Gregory the Great. He rejected the Henotikon of Emperor Zeno and in 484 excommunicated Patriarch Acacius of Constantinople, beginning the Acacian schism between Rome and the East. His surviving letters and decrees deal with this dispute and with church discipline, including the readmission of Christians in Africa who had lapsed under the Vandals.

Felix IV (489/490–530) was bishop of Rome from July 526 until his death in September 530. He was elected as the favoured candidate of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, who had imprisoned his predecessor, John I. Felix founded the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Roman Forum. He supported Caesarius of Arles against Semi-Pelagianism, and the Council of Orange (529) drew on his teaching on grace. Before he died he named Boniface II as his successor, which led to a disputed election against Dioscorus. Letters and decrees survive under his name, though some are spurious.

Gelasius I was bishop of Rome from 1 March 492 until his death on 19 November 496, and may earlier have drafted papal documents for his predecessor Felix III. He wrote many letters and treatises. He held a strict line on orthodoxy during the Acacian schism with Constantinople and asserted papal authority firmly. His letter Duo sunt to Emperor Anastasius I sets out the distinction between priestly authority and royal power, and it became highly influential. The Gelasian Decree and the Gelasian Sacramentary carry his name, but both are generally considered later works.

Hilarius (also Hilarus or Hilary) was bishop of Rome from 461 until his death on 29 February 468. Before that, as a legate of Pope Leo I at the Second Council of Ephesus in 449, he opposed the condemnation of Flavian of Constantinople and only narrowly escaped Dioscorus of Alexandria. He credited John the Evangelist with his escape and later built an oratory to him at the Lateran. As pope he upheld church discipline and canon law, settling disputes over jurisdiction among bishops in Gaul and Spain. His letters and synodal decrees survive.

Honorius I, born in Campania, was bishop of Rome from 625 until his death on 12 October 638. He backed the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons, sending Birinus to the West Saxons and granting the pallium to the archbishops of Canterbury and York. He also urged the Irish and British churches to adopt the Roman reckoning of Easter. His letters to Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople on the operations and will of Christ led the Third Council of Constantinople (681) to anathematize him posthumously for supporting Monothelitism.

Hormisdas (c. 450–523) was bishop of Rome from 514 until his death in 523. He was born at Frusino in Campania and was the father of the later Pope Silverius. The Acacian schism, which had divided Rome and Constantinople since 484, dominated his pontificate. He ended it in 519 when the Eastern bishops accepted the Formula of Hormisdas, a profession of faith that upheld the Council of Chalcedon and the authority of the Roman see. His surviving letters and decrees are an important source for church relations between East and West in the early sixth century.

Innocent I (Latin Innocentius I) was bishop of Rome from 401 until his death on 12 March 417. Bishops in both East and West turned to him to settle church disputes. He confirmed the privileges of the Archbishop of Thessalonica and defended the exiled John Chrysostom. In the Pelagian controversy he confirmed the rulings of the African synods. His surviving letters and decretals include a ruling on church discipline sent to the Bishop of Rouen and a well-known reply to Decentius of Gubbio on liturgical practice. These writings are important early sources for papal authority and canon law.

Pope John I (Latin Ioannes I; died 18 May 526) was bishop of Rome from 523 to 526. He is said to have come from Tuscany, near Siena. In 525, with the help of the monk Dionysius Exiguus, he played a part in standardizing how the Western Church calculated the date of Easter. The Ostrogothic king Theoderic sent him to Constantinople to seek better treatment for Arians in the East. When he returned to Ravenna, Theoderic imprisoned him on suspicion of conspiring with the emperor, and he died in captivity. Letters are attributed to him.

John III, born Catelinus, was bishop of Rome from 17 July 561 until his death on 13 July 574. He was from a Roman family. His pontificate came after the Byzantine reconquest of Italy and overlapped with the Lombard invasion of 568, a time of political disorder in Rome and the peninsula. Little reliable information survives about his activity, and no genuine writings of his are known. Texts that circulate under his name are pseudonymous and were attributed to him later.

John IV was bishop of Rome from 24 December 640 until his death on 12 October 642. He was a native of Dalmatia, and he became pope after a four-month vacancy. His surviving letters show two main concerns. He wrote to the clergy of Ireland and Scotland to correct their practice in dating Easter and to warn them against Pelagianism. He also condemned Monothelitism as heresy, defending the memory of his predecessor Honorius on this question. Tradition credits him with sending Abbot Martin to Dalmatia and Istria to ransom captives and recover relics of martyrs.

Julius I was bishop of Rome from 337 until his death in 352, during the Arian controversy. When Athanasius of Alexandria was deposed by Eastern bishops, Julius took him in, held a Roman synod that cleared him, and condemned his removal as unjust. His letter to the bishops gathered at Antioch defends this decision and asserts the authority of the Roman see over Eastern disputes. His letter to the clergy and people of Alexandria welcomes Athanasius's return to his see. Later tradition credits him with fixing 25 December as the date of Christmas.

Liberius (d. 366) was bishop of Rome from 352 until his death, succeeding Julius I. He refused to endorse the condemnation of Athanasius of Alexandria, and in 355 the emperor Constantius II exiled him to Thrace, while Felix II was installed in Rome. He returned around 358. Whether he had accepted a compromise formula and abandoned Athanasius to win his release has long been debated. Several of his letters survive. Ambrose records an address he gave when Ambrose's sister Marcellina took the veil of virginity. He is honoured as a saint in the East but not in the Roman Martyrology.

Lucius I was bishop of Rome from June 253 until his death on 5 March 254. He succeeded Cornelius and was sent into exile soon after his consecration, but was later allowed to return to Rome. Cyprian of Carthage wrote him a letter congratulating him on his return. Like Cornelius, he appears to have favoured readmitting the lapsed to communion after penance. Later tradition wrongly counted him as a martyr under Valerian, whose persecution began only after his death. None of his own writings survive, and texts bearing his name, such as a decretal in the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, are pseudonymous.

Marcellinus was bishop of Rome from 296 until his death in 304, during the Great Persecution under Diocletian. Some ancient sources claim he lapsed by offering sacrifice or handing over scriptures. Others, including Augustine of Hippo, rejected the charge, and the matter remains disputed. The legend of a council at Sinuessa that supposedly judged him comes from forgeries of the early sixth century. No genuine writings by him survive, and texts carrying his name are later pseudonymous works. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church and the Serbian Orthodox Church.

Marcellus I was bishop of Rome from May or June 308 until his death on 16 January 309. He was elected after a long vacancy following the death of Marcellinus. Under the emperor Maxentius he was banished from Rome. The cause was the unrest over the harsh penances he required of Christians who had lapsed during the recent persecution. He died the same year and Eusebius succeeded him. No genuine writings of his survive, and the letters later attributed to him are pseudonymous. He is venerated as a saint, and his relics lie in San Marcello al Corso in Rome.

Mark (Latin Marcus) was bishop of Rome from 18 January 336 until his death on 7 October of the same year. He succeeded Sylvester I. According to the Liber Pontificalis he was a Roman, the son of Priscus. The same source says he gave the bishop of Ostia the pallium and the right to consecrate new popes, and founded the Basilica of San Marco and a cemetery church over the Catacomb of Balbina, where he was buried. No genuine writings of his survive, and the letters later attributed to him are pseudonymous. His feast is kept on 7 October.

Miltiades, also called Melchiades and traditionally said to be of African origin, was bishop of Rome from 311 until his death in January 314. His pontificate saw Constantine's victory and the Edict of Milan (313), which gave Christianity legal status, and the Church received the imperial property at the Lateran. In 313 he presided over a synod in Rome that examined the Donatist dispute at Carthage. It upheld the bishop Caecilian and condemned Donatus and the practice of rebaptism. Later decrees circulated under his name are generally regarded as spurious.

Pelagius I was bishop of Rome from 16 April 556 until his death on 3 March 561. He was a Roman deacon and had served as papal apocrisiarius (envoy) in Constantinople. At first he opposed Emperor Justinian I's condemnation of the Three Chapters. He later accepted the emperor's position and was elected pope as Justinian's candidate, which was badly received in the West and caused schism in northern Italy. His surviving letters deal with church administration, the Three Chapters controversy and his efforts to defend his own orthodoxy.

Pelagius II was bishop of Rome from 26 November 579 until his death on 7 February 590. He was a Roman, said to be of Gothic descent, and was elected while the Lombards were besieging Rome. He sent the deacon Gregory, later Pope Gregory I, to Constantinople as his envoy to seek help from the emperor. His surviving letters and decrees include appeals to the bishops of Istria and Aquileia to end the Three Chapters schism. He also protested against the Patriarch of Constantinople's use of the title "ecumenical". He died during a plague and was succeeded by Gregory.

Sylvester I (Silvester) was bishop of Rome from 314 until his death on 31 December 335, during the reign of Constantine. Little reliable information about his life survives. His pontificate saw the Council of Arles (314), which condemned the Donatists, and the First Council of Nicaea (325), to which he sent legates. It also saw major churches built in Rome, including the Lateran basilica and Old St Peter's. Later legends made him the man who baptised Constantine and the recipient of the forged Donation of Constantine. Most letters and decrees attributed to him are of doubtful authenticity.

Simplicius was bishop of Rome from 468 until his death in March 483. He is traditionally said to have come from Tivoli. His pontificate saw the end of the Western Roman Empire in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. Simplicius defended the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychian (Monophysite) party in the East, and his letters deal with disputed episcopal successions at Alexandria and Antioch and with his relations with Acacius of Constantinople. He also tried to ease the effects of the Germanic invasions on the Church and ended the custom of consecrating bishops only in December.

Siricius (c. 334–399) was bishop of Rome from December 384 until his death on 26 November 399. Bishop Himerius of Tarragona had sent him questions, and in reply he issued the Directa decretal of 385. It set out rulings on baptism, penance, clerical celibacy and church discipline. His letters are the oldest papal decretals to survive complete. They include the letter to Himerius, a letter to Anysius of Thessalonica and a letter to the bishops of Africa. He is sometimes said to have been the first bishop of Rome to use the title pope.

Sixtus II, also written Xystus II, was bishop of Rome from 31 August 257 until his death on 6 August 258. He restored good relations with Cyprian of Carthage and the African and Eastern churches, which had broken down under his predecessor Stephen I over rebaptizing heretics. He was killed with seven deacons, including Lawrence, during Emperor Valerian's persecution, and was widely venerated as a martyr. No genuine writings of his survive. Later works were falsely attributed to him, notably the Sentences of Sextus, which Rufinus credited to him.

Sixtus III, also called Xystus III, was bishop of Rome from 31 July 432 until his death on 18 August 440. He succeeded Celestine I and was followed by Leo I. As a Roman priest he received letters from Augustine of Hippo on the Pelagian controversy. As pope he supported the 433 reconciliation between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch after the Council of Ephesus. His pontificate brought a period of major building in Rome, including the rebuilding of the basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore. Letters and decrees ascribed to him survive.

Stephen I was Bishop of Rome from 254 until his death in 257. He is best known for his dispute with Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea over rebaptism. Stephen held that baptism given by heretics or schismatics was valid and should not be repeated; converts needed only the laying on of hands. None of his own letters survive, and his views are known mainly through Cyprian's correspondence. Later writings were falsely attributed to him. He is venerated as a saint, and some accounts call him a martyr, though this is doubtful.

Symmachus (died 19 July 514) was bishop of Rome from 22 November 498 until his death. He was born in Sardinia and served as a deacon of the Roman Church. On the day of his election a rival faction with Byzantine sympathies chose the archpriest Laurentius, which began the Laurentian schism. It divided the clergy, the Senate and the people of Rome. The Ostrogothic king Theodoric decided in favour of Symmachus, but the dispute lasted until about 506. His surviving letters and synodal decrees cover church discipline, papal elections and relations with the churches of Gaul and the East.

Vigilius was bishop of Rome from 537 until his death in 555. A Roman aristocrat, he served as deacon and papal apocrisiarius in Constantinople. With Empress Theodora's backing, he became pope after Silverius was deposed. The Three Chapters controversy dominated his pontificate. Taken to Constantinople in 545 under pressure from Justinian I, he wavered over condemning the Chapters and finally accepted the condemnation after the Second Council of Constantinople (553). He died in Sicily on his way back to Rome. His letters and decrees survive.

Zosimus was bishop of Rome from 18 March 417 until his death on 26 December 418. According to tradition he was of Greek origin. His short pontificate was marked by controversy. In Gaul he gave strong rulings for the see of Arles against Vienne and other churches, but did not settle the dispute. In the Pelagian controversy he first seemed to favour Pelagius and Caelestius. After pressure from the African bishops, he condemned them in 418 in his Epistola tractoria. His letters and decrees survive.

Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius was a Latin poet of the age of Constantine I, active roughly between 315 and 335, possibly a native of Africa. He is usually identified with the Publilius Optatianus who was prefect of Rome in 329 and 333. After being banished for reasons that remain unknown, he sent Constantine a panegyric collection of poems and was allowed to return. He is known for elaborate pattern poems in which highlighted letters form pictures, monograms and further verses, some of them with Christian symbols such as the Chi-Rho. A letter to the emperor and Constantine's reply also survive.

Potamius (fl. c. 343–360) was the first recorded bishop of Lisbon (Olisipo), in Roman Hispania. He took part in the Council of Sirmium in 357, where he supported the Arian-leaning formula of that year. At other points in his career he took the Nicene side, so his doctrinal position appears to have changed over time. After Hosius of Corduba, he is the earliest known Christian prose writer of the Iberian Peninsula. His surviving writings include letters and two sermons, on Lazarus and on the martyrdom of Isaiah, which are known for their elaborate and often obscure rhetorical style.

Primasius (died c. 560) was bishop of Hadrumetum, in modern Tunisia, and primate of the North African province of Byzacena. He was in Constantinople during the Three Chapters Controversy under Emperor Justinian. His main work is a commentary on the Book of Revelation in five books. Modern scholars value it because it draws on the lost commentary of the Donatist writer Tyconius. A commentary on the Pauline epistles has also been printed under his name, but who wrote it is doubtful. The African theologian Junillus is said to have been one of his students.

Priscillian (c. 340–c. 385) was a wealthy layman from Gallaecia in Roman Hispania who led a strict ascetic movement. His followers' practices were condemned at the Council of Zaragoza in 380, yet he became bishop of Ávila that same year. Opposed by other Spanish bishops, he was tried at Trier on a charge of sorcery and executed under the emperor Maximus. He is often called the first Christian executed for heresy. Eleven tractates attributed to him or his circle were rediscovered in 1885. His canons on the Pauline epistles survive in a version revised by a bishop named Peregrinus.

Faltonia Betitia Proba was a Roman Christian poet of the fourth century. She came from one of Rome's most influential aristocratic families, and her exact dates are uncertain, with birth placed around 306–322 and death around 353–370. After converting to Christianity she composed the Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi, a cento made of lines taken from Virgil and rearranged to tell stories from the Old and New Testaments, centred on the life of Jesus. The poem circulated widely and was used in teaching. Jerome is often thought to have criticised it, while Isidore of Seville and Boccaccio praised her ingenuity.

Proclus (c. 390–446) was archbishop of Constantinople from 434 until his death. He was a celebrated preacher and played a central part in the Nestorian controversy. His homily on the Virgin Mary as Theotokos, preached before Nestorius around 428–429, is an early landmark of Marian theology. As archbishop he wrote the Tome to the Armenians, a statement of Christology, and in 438 he brought the relics of John Chrysostom back to the capital. His homilies and letters survive in Greek and in early translations. He is venerated as a saint in both Eastern and Western churches.

Procopius of Caesarea (c. 500 – c. 565) was a Greek scholar and historian from Caesarea in Palestine and the leading historian of the sixth century. He served as an adviser to the general Belisarius and went with him on Emperor Justinian I's campaigns against Persia, the Vandals in North Africa and the Goths in Italy. His History of the Wars describes these conflicts. On Buildings praises Justinian's construction projects. The Secret History, unpublished during his lifetime, is a fierce attack on Justinian, Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina.

Procopius of Gaza (c. 465 – c. 528) was a Christian sophist and rhetorician, and one of the leading figures of the rhetorical school of Gaza, where he taught Choricius among others. His secular works include letters, declamations and a panegyric on Emperor Anastasius I. He is best known for his biblical commentaries, which gathered and condensed the interpretations of earlier Greek Fathers on the Octateuch, the books of Kings and Chronicles, Isaiah, Proverbs and the Song of Songs. Because of this method, he is often counted among the earliest compilers of exegetical catenae.

Procopius the Deacon (Latin Procopius Diaconus) was a Byzantine Greek churchman and writer, active in the first half of the ninth century. Very little is known about his life beyond his rank as a deacon. He is remembered as the author of encomia, rhetorical speeches in praise of saints, and other short pieces. These belong to the Middle Byzantine tradition of festal and hagiographical oratory. He should not be confused with the sixth-century historian Procopius of Caesarea or with Procopius of Gaza.

Prosper was a former Manichaean who converted to Catholic Christianity in the Latin West. He is known only from a short formal text of abjuration, the Anathematismi et fidei catholicae professio. In it he condemns Mani and the main teachings of Manichaeism and then professes the Catholic faith. Formulas like this were used when Manichaeans were received into the Church. The text is usually dated to about 526–530, though its exact date and setting are uncertain, and nothing else is known about his life.

Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390 – c. 455), also called Prosper Tiro, was a Latin Christian writer, probably a layman, from southern Gaul. He was a disciple of Augustine of Hippo. Around 428–429 he wrote to Augustine about opposition to his teaching on grace among the monks of Marseille. He went on to defend Augustinian doctrine in works such as the poem De ingratis and Contra collatorem, a reply to John Cassian. He later worked in Rome and continued Jerome's Chronicle. De vocatione omnium gentium is often attributed to him. The axiom "lex orandi, lex credendi" is associated with him.

Protadius (died c. 624) was bishop of Besançon in Merovingian Gaul in the early seventh century, active roughly from 614 to 624, and is venerated locally as a saint. Little is known for certain about his life. Several Latin texts have been attributed to him: a liturgical work, a charter for the restoration of the chapter of Saint-Étienne at Besançon, and a catalogue of the bishops of the church of Besançon. The authenticity and dating of these attributions are uncertain, and some of the texts may be later compositions.

Proterius (died 457) was Patriarch of Alexandria from 451 to 457. After the Council of Chalcedon deposed Dioscorus, Proterius was installed in his place. Much of the Egyptian population opposed the council, and his patriarchate was troubled throughout. After Dioscorus died, the anti-Chalcedonian party consecrated Timothy Ailuros as a rival bishop. Proterius was killed by a mob in Alexandria in 457, and the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches honour him as a hieromartyr. A letter he wrote to Pope Leo I about the date of Easter survives in a Latin version by Dionysius Exiguus.

Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (348–after 405) was a Latin Christian poet from the Roman province of Tarraconensis in Hispania. His birthplace is uncertain; Caesaraugusta, Tarraco and Calagurris have all been proposed. He worked as a lawyer and provincial governor and held a post at the imperial court before turning to religious poetry late in life. His works include the Cathemerinon, hymns for the hours of the day; the Peristephanon, on the martyrs; the doctrinal poems Apotheosis and Hamartigenia; and the Psychomachia, an allegory of the soul's struggle between virtues and vices that strongly influenced medieval literature.

Pseudo-Ambrose is the conventional name for the authors of Latin writings that were handed down under the name of Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), but are not his work or are of doubtful authenticity. The group is not one author. It brings together treatises, sermons and letters of different dates and origins, including a tract on the Trinity and the Apostles' Creed, a work on the dignity of the priesthood, and an exhortation addressed to a consecrated virgin. Ambrose's great authority helped these texts circulate widely in the medieval West. Most of their real authors and dates remain unknown.

Pseudo-Anastasius is the conventional name for the unknown author or authors of Latin writings wrongly or doubtfully attributed to Pope Anastasius I, bishop of Rome from 399 to 401. Anastasius is known mainly for his part in the Origenist controversy and for letters on church discipline. The material under his name is chiefly two letters that are now considered spurious. Such papal attributions were common in early medieval canonical collections, because they gave rulings on discipline and doctrine the authority of an early pope. Who wrote the letters, and when, is not known.

Pseudo-Apollinaris is the name modern scholars give to the unknown authors of Greek writings once attributed to Apollinaris of Laodicea (died c. 390), the bishop and theologian whose views on Christ's humanity were condemned as Apollinarism. The best-known work in this group is the Metaphrasis Psalmorum. It retells the whole Psalter in Homeric-style dactylic hexameters. Ancient manuscripts credited it to Apollinaris, but most modern scholars think an anonymous Christian poet wrote it later, probably in the fifth century. The authorship and date are still debated. It is an important example of late antique Christian verse paraphrase of the Bible.

Pseudo-Athanasius is the conventional name for the authors of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373). These texts do not form a single corpus. Each is an independent work with its own date, genre and purpose, and Athanasius's name was often added to give it authority. Besides Greek, such pseudepigrapha survive in Latin, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Arabic, Ethiopic, Georgian and Slavonic. Some are translations and others are original compositions. They include Trinitarian treatises against the Sabellians, homilies on the Passion, the Quaestiones on Scripture, the Synopsis of Sacred Scripture, Coptic discourses and the Athanasian Creed.

Pseudo-Augustine is the name scholars give, collectively, to the authors of works falsely or doubtfully attributed to Augustine of Hippo (354–430). Augustine listed many of his own writings in his Retractationes, and his disciple Possidius tried to catalogue them all in his Indiculus. Even so, Augustine's great authority drew many other texts under his name. They include numerous sermons, later grouped by editors as "suppositious" sermons, along with exegetical, ascetic and devotional treatises. Their dates range from late antiquity to the Middle Ages, and their authors are mostly anonymous.

Pseudo-Barnabas is the name given to the unknown author of the Epistle of Barnabas, a Greek Christian treatise usually dated between about 70 and 135. The author is counted among the Apostolic Fathers. Clement of Alexandria and other early writers credited the work to Barnabas, Paul's companion, but most modern scholars reject this. The epistle reads the Hebrew Scriptures allegorically as prophecies of Christ and argues that the Jews misunderstood their law by taking it literally. Some early churches treated it as scripture, and Codex Sinaiticus includes it after Revelation.

Pseudo-Basil is the name scholars give to the anonymous authors of texts falsely or doubtfully attributed to Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379). The corpus is varied and comes from many periods. It includes books IV–V of Against Eunomius, which were added to Basil's three authentic books. It also contains ascetic constitutions and admonitions, homilies, canons, apocryphal letters and liturgical texts. Some pieces are now credited to other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus and Basil of Ancyra. Many survive only in Coptic, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Slavonic or Latin versions.

Pseudo-Benedict is the conventional name for the unknown authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the monastic founder of Monte Cassino and author of the Rule. The writings include a sermon circulated under his name, a spurious letter addressed to Saint Remigius of Reims, and a sermon on the death of his disciple Placidus. That sermon belongs to the later legend of Placidus's martyrdom. The authors and dates of these texts are uncertain. They show how Benedict's reputation drew later compositions to his name.

Pseudo-Boethius is the name given to Latin writings that were attributed to the Roman philosopher Boethius (c. 480–524) but whose authenticity is doubtful or rejected. They include the medieval geometrical compilations known as the Geometria Boethii, which combine excerpts from Euclid's Elements with Roman surveying material. These may preserve fragments of a lost Boethian translation of Euclid, but they were assembled centuries after his death. The short creed-like treatise Brevis fidei Christianae complexio, transmitted with his theological tractates, has also been questioned, although many scholars now accept it as genuine.

Pseudo-Boniface is the conventional name for the author or authors of Latin letters falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Boniface I, bishop of Rome from 418 to 422. Boniface's genuine correspondence deals with papal authority, the disputed papal election that brought him to office, and jurisdiction over Illyricum and Gaul. Other letters were later added under his name in canonical collections, and their authenticity is rejected or uncertain. Who wrote them and when is not known. They matter mainly for the history of papal letters and of canon law.

Pseudo-Boniface II is the name given to Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Boniface II, bishop of Rome from 530 to 532. The main piece is a letter to a bishop Eulalius, called "of Alexandria" in its title. It describes a church that had broken communion with Rome being reconciled and condemning its earlier leaders. The letter is usually judged spurious and is associated with medieval collections of forged papal decretals. Its date and origin are uncertain. Such texts were written to support claims of papal authority.

Pseudo-Caesarius of Arles is the conventional name for the unknown authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Caesarius, bishop of Arles (d. 542). Caesarius was a widely copied preacher whose sermons circulated freely and were often reworked. As a result, many anonymous sermons, admonitions and letters from Gaul and elsewhere were later passed down under his name. The authorship and dates of these texts vary and are often uncertain. They include the Epistola ad quosdam Germanos. This group is separate from the Greek Pseudo-Caesarius linked to Caesarius of Nazianzus.

Pseudo-Caesarius is the name modern scholars give to the anonymous Greek author of the Erotapokriseis. This is a set of four dialogues in question-and-answer form that was falsely attributed to Caesarius of Nazianzus, the physician brother of Gregory of Nazianzus who died about 369. The work actually dates from the mid-sixth century. Its more than two hundred questions cover the Trinity and Christology, the interpretation of difficult biblical passages, cosmology and natural science, and arguments against astrology and fate. It also preserves valuable ethnographic notices, including an early Greek mention of the Slavs.

Pseudo-Caius is the name for Latin writings falsely attributed to Caius, bishop of Rome in the late third century (traditionally c. 283–296). The main text under his name is the Epistola ad Felicem episcopum, a letter to a bishop named Felix. It belongs to the forged papal decretals of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, which was compiled in the Frankish realm in the mid-ninth century. These letters presented later church law as rulings of early popes, especially on the rights of bishops and their protection from accusation. They had a lasting influence on medieval canon law.

Pseudo-Cassiodorus is the name given to the unknown authors of Latin works that were handed down under the name of Cassiodorus (c. 485–c. 585), the Roman statesman and founder of the monastery of Vivarium, but which are now judged spurious or doubtful. The writings include an exposition of the Song of Songs and two grammatical and rhetorical works: a treatise on speech and the eight parts of speech, and a handbook of figures and tropes. They were attached to Cassiodorus because of his reputation for biblical exegesis and for teaching the liberal arts. Their actual authors and dates are uncertain.

Pseudo-Celestine is the name scholars use for the unknown author or authors of Coptic writings falsely attributed to Celestine I, bishop of Rome from 422 to 432. The best-known work is an encomium on Saint Victor, the soldier-martyr venerated in Egypt as Victor Stratelates, son of Romanos. It belongs to a large body of Coptic homilies and panegyrics that were credited to famous early Church fathers to give them authority. Its real author and date are unknown. It was probably written in Egypt well after Celestine's lifetime.

Pseudo-Chromatius is the conventional name for writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia in northern Italy (died c. 407). Chromatius was a friend and patron of Jerome and Rufinus, and his own sermons and tractates on Matthew often circulated under other famous names. In the same way, texts by other authors were sometimes passed down under his name. This group also includes references to his lost works. Who wrote the misattributed pieces, and when, is mostly unknown.

Pseudo-Claudianus Mamertus is the name given to Latin Christian poems that were once attributed to Claudianus Mamertus (died c. 474), the priest of Vienne in Gaul and author of the treatise De statu animae, but are not accepted as his work. Sidonius Apollinaris praised Mamertus as a poet, and this reputation probably drew anonymous verse to his name in manuscripts and early printed editions. The authorship and dates of these carmina are uncertain, and scholars generally assign them to other or unknown late antique writers.

Pseudo-Clement is the conventional name for the various anonymous authors of early Christian writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Clement of Rome, the late first-century bishop. They include the so-called Second Epistle of Clement, an anonymous homily probably from the mid-second century, and two letters on virginity, which survive complete in Syriac and are usually dated to the third century. The largest group is the Clementine literature: a fourth-century romance about Clement's travels with the apostle Peter, preserved as the Homilies and the Recognitions. The Homilies are prefaced by letters of Peter and Clement to James and by the Contestatio.

Pseudo-Constantine is the name given to Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Constantine the Great, Roman emperor from 306 to 337. The best known is the Constitutum Constantini, or Donation of Constantine. This forged decree, probably composed in the 8th century, claims that Constantine granted authority over Rome and the western empire to the pope. Lorenzo Valla showed in 1439–1440 that it was a forgery. The group also includes a letter falsely ascribed to Constantine and addressed to Pope Melchiades (Miltiades), and an alleged treaty between Constantine and King Tiridates of Armenia.

Pseudo-Cyprian is the conventional name for the anonymous authors of Latin works wrongly attributed to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage (d. 258). These writings have no shared author or transmission history. Most are not deliberate forgeries; they became linked to Cyprian early in their copying, and many were accepted as genuine until modern times. They include treatises and sermons from the third and fourth centuries, such as Ad Novatianum, De singularitate clericorum, On the Glory of Martyrdom and Exhortation to Repentance. They are valuable evidence for early Latin Christianity in North Africa and elsewhere.

Pseudo-Cyril of Alexandria is the name scholars use for the unknown authors of writings wrongly or doubtfully attributed to Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. The Greek works include the treatise De sacrosancta Trinitate, a systematic account of Trinitarian and Christological doctrine. It is now usually attributed to the Byzantine scholar Joseph the Philosopher. Another Greek work is the homily De exitu animi, on the soul's departure from the body. Other spurious pieces circulated under Cyril's name in Greek, and further homilies and commentaries were assigned to him in Coptic and Arabic.

Pseudo-Cyril of Jerusalem is the name scholars give to the unknown authors of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem (c. 313–386), known for his Catechetical Lectures. The group covers texts of different dates, languages and origins. Besides Greek pieces gathered among the works "supposed" to be Cyril's, it includes many later Coptic, Arabic and Ethiopic homilies on Christ's passion and resurrection, on the Virgin Mary and her Dormition, and on Mary Magdalene. Cyril's name gave these texts authority.

Pseudo-Damasus is the name given to Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Damasus I, bishop of Rome from 366 to 384. Damasus was known for his verse epigrams on the martyrs, and his reputation drew later texts to his name. These include letters, among them spurious correspondence with Jerome, as well as creedal and canonical documents and poems. Most were written after his lifetime, some in the early Middle Ages. Their authors and dates are mostly uncertain, and scholars still disagree about how authentic some pieces are.

Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite is the name given to the anonymous author of the Corpus Areopagiticum, a group of Greek writings probably composed in Syria in the late fifth or early sixth century. The author presents himself as Dionysius, the Athenian convert of Paul mentioned in Acts 17:34. The corpus includes the Celestial Hierarchy, the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, the Divine Names, the Mystical Theology and ten letters. It draws heavily on the Neoplatonism of Proclus. Its accounts of angelic ranks, liturgical symbolism and apophatic, or negative, theology deeply influenced Byzantine and medieval Latin thought.

Pseudo-Eleutherius of Tournai is the name given to the author or authors of Latin sermons wrongly attributed to Saint Eleutherius, traditionally the first bishop of Tournai, who died in the early sixth century. The sermons deal with doctrinal subjects and the feasts of the Church year. Medieval tradition at Tournai, which promoted the cult of Eleutherius, transmitted them under his name. Scholars generally regard them as much later compositions, though their exact date and authorship remain uncertain.

Pseudo-Elpis is the name used for Latin liturgical hymns traditionally ascribed to Elpis, who in late tradition is described as a Sicilian woman and the wife of the philosopher Boethius, active in the early sixth century. The writings in question are hymns for the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, among them the hymn beginning "Aurea luce" sung in the Western Office. Modern scholars consider the attribution to Elpis doubtful or legendary, and the hymns' actual authorship and date are uncertain.

Pseudo-Ephrem is the conventional name for the authors of the many writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), the deacon and hymnographer of Nisibis and Edessa. His fame was so great that for centuries Christian writers produced hundreds of homilies, hymns, ascetic exhortations and apocalyptic texts under his name. The best known include the Syriac and Latin apocalypses of Pseudo-Ephrem. Much of this literature survives in Greek, and from there it passed into Coptic, Latin, Slavonic and other languages. Authorship and dates vary from text to text and are often uncertain.

Pseudo-Epiphanius is the name given to the anonymous authors of Greek writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Epiphanius of Salamis, the fourth-century bishop of Cyprus. The works are of different dates and origins. They include a homily on the burial of the Lord for Holy Saturday, which describes Christ's descent to the dead and his meeting with Adam; its date is uncertain. Other works are a recension of the Lives of the Prophets and lists of legends about the apostles and disciples, the latter usually dated to around the eighth century.

Pseudo-Eucherius is the name used for Latin writings that were transmitted under the name of Eucherius, bishop of Lyon in the fifth century, but whose authorship is false or doubtful. The group includes a short description of Jerusalem and Judaea, De situ Hierusolimitanae urbis, which some scholars accept as genuine; a letter addressed to a priest named Philo; and various homilies. Many sermons attributed to Eucherius belong to the southern Gaulish preaching collections. Later medieval writers also had works ascribed to him, which reflects his reputation as an exegete.

Pseudo-Eusebius is the name given to the unknown author or authors of Latin letters falsely attributed to Pope Eusebius, bishop of Rome briefly around 309 or 310. The best-known of these spurious epistles belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal decrees produced in the Frankish kingdom in the mid-ninth century. Like the other forgeries in that collection, they deal with church discipline, the rights of accused bishops and the authority of the Roman see. They tell us nothing reliable about the historical Eusebius.

Pseudo-Eusebius of Vercelli is the name for Latin writings attributed, falsely or doubtfully, to Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli in northern Italy (died c. 371). Eusebius was a leading opponent of Arianism and was exiled after the Council of Milan in 355. His reputation as a defender of Nicene orthodoxy drew later anonymous doctrinal texts to his name. Among them is the De sancta Trinitate confessio, a short profession of faith in the Trinity. Its true author and date are uncertain.

Pseudo-Eustathius of Antioch is the name given to the unknown author or authors of Greek writings falsely attributed to Eustathius, the anti-Arian bishop of Antioch deposed around 330. The best-known is a commentary on the six days of creation in Genesis, written between about 375 and 500. It cannot be Eustathius's work because it draws on Basil the Great's Hexaemeron homilies of around 370 and calls Eusebius of Caesarea, his opponent, "holy." The commentary also preserves extracts from the lost writings of Alexander Polyhistor and is an early witness to the Physiologus.

Pseudo-Eutychian is the name given to the Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Eutychian, bishop of Rome in the later third century (traditionally c. 275–283). None of his genuine writings survive. The pieces under his name are a letter and short decrees on church discipline. They belong mainly to the forged papal letters of the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, which assigned legal rulings to early popes to give them ancient authority. They later passed into canon-law collections and printed editions of the councils, such as Labbe's.

Pseudo-Felix is the name given to the authors of Latin letters falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Felix I, bishop of Rome from about 269 to 274. Nothing Felix himself wrote survives with certainty. A doctrinal fragment ascribed to him and cited at the Council of Ephesus in 431 is generally regarded as an Apollinarian forgery. Other letters under his name belong to the forged papal decretals of the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian collection. Together they show how later writers used early popes' authority to support doctrinal and disciplinary claims.

Pseudo-Flavian is the name used for the unknown author of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to a bishop named Flavian, sometimes identified with Flavian of Constantinople (d. 449). The main surviving work is an encomium on Demetrius, the late-second- and early-third-century bishop of Alexandria. It is preserved in Coptic and belongs to the Egyptian tradition of panegyrics on the great patriarchs of Alexandria. The real author is unknown and the date is uncertain. The attribution probably served to lend the text the authority of a famous name.

Pseudo-Fulgentius is the name scholars give to the authors of Latin works falsely or doubtfully attributed to Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 467–533), the North African bishop known for his writings against Arianism and in defence of Augustine's teaching on grace. His reputation as an Augustinian theologian drew anonymous texts to his name. They include a treatise on predestination and grace and a collection of eighty sermons, wrongly ascribed to him, whose pieces come from various authors and periods. Their actual authorship and dates are mostly uncertain.

Pseudo-Gelasius is the conventional name for the authors of Latin texts falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Gelasius I (492–496). Gelasius wrote a great deal and had a strong reputation as a legislator, so later writers attached his name to other material. The best-known example is the Gelasian Decree, a list of accepted and rejected books that reached its final form between 519 and 553 and may come from Gaul. The name also covers canons ascribed to Gelasius that circulated in early medieval collections of church law. The so-called Gelasian Sacramentary was likewise later linked to his name.

Pseudo-Germanus of Paris is the name given to the anonymous author of the Expositio brevis antiquae liturgiae Gallicanae. This commentary on the Gallican liturgy survives in the form of two letters and was traditionally attributed to Germanus, bishop of Paris (d. 576). Most scholars reject that attribution and date the work to around the late seventh or eighth century, probably in Gaul. It explains the parts of the Mass and other rites allegorically. Because so little else survives about the Gallican Rite before the Carolingian shift to Roman liturgy, it is a key witness to how that rite was celebrated.

Pseudo-Gregory of Nazianzus is the conventional name for the unknown authors of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), the Cappadocian Father and archbishop of Constantinople. Gregory's fame as a theologian and orator drew many texts to his name. They differ in date, origin and genre, and their authors are mostly unidentified. Among them are a treatise On the Orthodox Faith, a fragment of an oration against astrologers, Oration 35 on the martyrs and against the Arians, which is usually judged spurious, and the Liturgy of St Gregory, an anaphora used in the Alexandrian tradition.

Pseudo-Gregory of Nyssa is the conventional name for the authors of Greek writings transmitted under the name of Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, whose authorship is rejected or doubted. They are works of different dates and origins that were later drawn into his corpus. They include a treatise on humanity made in the image and likeness of God, an anti-Arian and anti-Sabellian Trinitarian tract, a homily on the Presentation of the Lord, an encomium of Ephrem the Syrian, and the Testimonies against the Jews, a 4th- or 5th-century collection.

Pseudo-Gregory of Tours is the name given to Latin writings that were transmitted under the name of Gregory of Tours (c. 538–594) but are falsely or doubtfully attributed to him. Gregory was the Gallo-Roman bishop of Tours best known for his Histories of the Franks and his books of miracles. Because of his reputation as a historian and hagiographer, other anonymous texts were joined to his corpus over time. Their authors, dates and places of origin are mostly uncertain, and each work has to be assessed separately.

Pseudo-Gregory Thaumaturgus is the name given to Greek writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus ("the Wonderworker"), the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus and pupil of Origen. His reputation for orthodoxy drew later texts to his name. These include short treatises on the Trinity and the soul, homilies on feasts and saints, and doctrinal statements. The Sectional Confession of Faith (Kata meros pistis) is generally assigned to Apollinaris of Laodicea. The Twelve Topics on the Faith are also of later date. Their authorship is otherwise uncertain.

Pseudo-Gregory the Great is the conventional name for the authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604). Because of Gregory's great authority as a teacher, preacher and reformer of worship, medieval copyists attached his name to many texts. Among them is a group of liturgical hymns traditionally ascribed to him, whose authorship remains uncertain. Another is the Concordia quorumdam testimoniorum S. Scripturae, a short treatise reconciling passages of Scripture that appear to contradict one another. Scholars have also questioned whether some works long accepted as Gregory's, such as the Dialogues, are authentic.

Pseudo-Hegesippus is the conventional name for the anonymous author of De excidio Hierosolymitano ("On the Destruction of Jerusalem"). This Latin Christian adaptation of Josephus's Jewish War in five books was probably written around 370. The name "Hegesippus" seems to come from a corrupted form of "Josephus", and the work has nothing to do with the second-century chronicler. Some have attributed it to Ambrose of Milan, but authorship remains disputed. The author condenses and reworks Josephus, presenting the fall of Jerusalem as divine punishment of the Jews.

Pseudo-Hilary of Arles is the name for Latin writings that have been attributed, wrongly or doubtfully, to Hilary, bishop of Arles (died 449). They include a sermon on a miracle of Saint Genesius, the martyr of Arles; a poem for the feast of the Maccabean martyrs; and a hexameter poem on the creation story in Genesis, addressed to a Pope Leo. These pieces come from Gaul in late antiquity, but who wrote them and exactly when is unknown. Some manuscripts link the poems with other authors, including Hilary of Poitiers.

Pseudo-Hilary is the name given to the unknown authors of Latin writings once attributed to Hilary of Poitiers (died c. 367), the bishop and opponent of Arianism, but now judged not to be his or only doubtfully his. The group includes several short biblical poems in Latin verse, probably from late antiquity. In Genesin ad Leonem papam retells the creation story and is addressed to a Pope Leo. De martyrio Maccabaeorum tells of the Maccabean martyrs, and De Evangelio treats Gospel themes. Their authorship and dates are uncertain.

Pseudo-Hippolytus is the conventional name for the author or authors of Greek writings that were transmitted under the name of Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170 – c. 235) but are spurious or of doubtful authenticity. The corpus includes the fragments Against Beron and Helix, a Discourse on the End of the World and on Antichrist, a homily on the Holy Theophany, and lists of the Twelve and the Seventy Apostles. Most of these works are thought to date from well after Hippolytus's lifetime, though their exact dates and origins are uncertain.

Pseudo-Ignatius is the name given to the writings falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the bishop martyred in the early second century. The main body is the Long Recension. In it, a fourth-century writer, probably in Syria, expanded Ignatius' seven genuine letters and added spurious ones to the Tarsians, Antiochians, Philippians, Hero, and Mary of Cassobelae. Many scholars think he also compiled the Apostolic Constitutions. His Christology is debated, and some see Arian or Apollinarian leanings in it. A later, separate Latin forgery is the short correspondence of Ignatius with the apostle John and the Virgin Mary.

Pseudo-Innocent is the name used for letters and other documents falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Innocent I, bishop of Rome from 401 to 417. Innocent's genuine correspondence carried great authority in the Latin Church, especially on discipline and church order, and this encouraged later writers to put texts out under his name. These spurious letters usually circulated beside the authentic ones in collections of papal decretals and canon law. Their authors and dates are mostly unknown, and how authentic particular items are has long been debated by scholars.

Pseudo-Isidore is the conventional name for the unknown Carolingian forger, or group of forgers, active around the middle of the ninth century. He probably worked in the province of Reims and drew on the library of Corbie. His best-known product, the False Decretals, claims to have been compiled by one Isidorus Mercator. It mixes authentic material with more than ninety forged letters of early popes. Related forgeries include the capitularies of Benedictus Levita. The forgeries aimed to protect bishops from accusation and deposition, safeguard church property and strengthen papal jurisdiction, and they deeply influenced medieval canon law.

Pseudo-Isidore of Seville is a conventional label for Latin writings handed down under the name of Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), archbishop of Seville, but now judged spurious or of doubtful authenticity. Isidore's great reputation drew anonymous texts of various dates and origins into his corpus. These include poems ascribed to him, a commentary on the Song of Songs, and the moral treatise De conflictu vitiorum et virtutum, which is now usually credited to the eighth-century monk Ambrosius Autpertus. The label is distinct from the ninth-century forger of the False Decretals, also called Pseudo-Isidore.

Pseudo-Jerome is the conventional name for the many anonymous authors whose Latin writings were falsely or doubtfully circulated under the name of Saint Jerome (d. 420). Because Jerome was so highly regarded, medieval copyists often attached his name to letters, sermons, biblical commentaries and short reference works. These texts date from late antiquity through the Carolingian period and later. They include the ninth-century letter to Paula and Eustochium on the Assumption of Mary, a Handbook on the Apocalypse probably written by a late seventh-century Irish author, brief lives of the apostles, and spurious letters addressed to a certain Desiderius.

Pseudo-Chrysostom is the name scholars use for the anonymous authors of works once falsely or doubtfully attributed to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (died 407). Because more than 500 of his genuine sermons survive, most of these works are homilies, many of them for feasts and the liturgical year. Some identified authors include Apollinaris of Laodicea, Severian of Gabala and an Anomoean preacher. The Latin Opus imperfectum in Matthaeum is the work of an Arian. Chrysostom's prestige ensured that these texts survived and were widely translated, including into Armenian, Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic and Old Nubian.

Pseudo-John is the name given to the unknown Greek author of a Life of Epiphanius of Salamis (d. 403). The work presents itself as written by John, a disciple and companion of Epiphanius, and is followed by an appendix credited to Polybius, another supposed disciple. Scholars treat it as a later, largely legendary hagiography rather than an eyewitness account. When it was written is uncertain, and estimates range from the fifth century to the early medieval period. Nothing is known of the real author.

Pseudo-John III is the conventional name for the authors of Latin letters falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope John III, bishop of Rome from 561 to 574. The best known is a letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal letters made in the Frankish kingdom in the mid-ninth century to support the rights of bishops and the authority of Rome. A letter to Eraldus, bishop of Vienne, is also transmitted under John's name, but it is not considered authentic.

Pseudo-Julius is the name used for a group of writings falsely attributed to Pope Julius I (bishop of Rome 337–352). They were actually written in the later fourth century by Apollinaris of Laodicea or his followers. After Apollinarianism was condemned, these letters and statements on the incarnation circulated under the names of respected orthodox figures, Julius among them. They stress the single nature of the incarnate Word and were later quoted in the Christological controversies of the fifth and sixth centuries. Leontius of Byzantium was among those who exposed them as forgeries.

Pseudo-Julius Africanus is the name used for writings falsely attributed to Sextus Julius Africanus, the early third-century Christian chronographer. The best-known is a Greek legend, the Narrative of Events Happening in Persia on the Birth of Christ. It tells of wonders in a Persian temple, where pagan idols announce the virgin birth, and of the journey of the Magi. The narrative is connected with the Disputation at the Sasanian Court and is much later than Africanus, probably from late antiquity. Its exact date and origin are uncertain.

Pseudo-Justin is the name scholars use for the anonymous authors of Greek works falsely or doubtfully attributed to the second-century apologist Justin Martyr. They were not one person, and the writings come from different periods, roughly the third to the fifth century. They include the Exhortation to the Greeks (Cohortatio ad Graecos), the short Discourse to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos), and On the Sole Government of God (De monarchia), which cites a poem attributed to Orpheus. Others are the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, the treatise On the Resurrection and the Exposition of the Right Faith, which may be by Theodoret of Cyrrhus.

Pseudo-Juvencus is the name given to Latin poems falsely or doubtfully ascribed to Juvencus, the fourth-century Spanish priest whose Evangeliorum libri quattuor is the earliest surviving Latin epic paraphrase of the Gospels. Because Juvencus was the model for Christian biblical epic, later verse in the same style was sometimes placed under his name. One example is the Triumphus Christi heroicus, a heroic poem on Christ's triumph that was printed among his works. The real author and date of these pieces are uncertain.

Pseudo-Leo is the conventional name for the authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Leo the Great, bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. Leo's authority as a preacher and as the author of the Tome made his name attractive to later compilers. The body of writings includes sermons transmitted under his name, along with letters and canonical texts whose authenticity scholars have rejected or questioned. Their authors and dates vary and are mostly unknown. These texts shed light on how Leo's reputation was used in later preaching and church law.

Pseudo-Leo VI is the name for writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to the Byzantine emperor Leo VI the Wise (reigned 886–912), who had a reputation as a scholar and seer. The best known are the Oracles of Leo the Wise, a Greek collection of short, obscure prophecies, each paired with a symbolic image. They concern the fate of emperors and of Constantinople. The oracles were put together well after Leo's lifetime, probably in the later Byzantine period, from older material. Explanatory paraphrases were added to them, and they were widely read and reinterpreted after the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Pseudo-Lucifer is the conventional name for the author or authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Lucifer of Cagliari. Lucifer was a fourth-century Sardinian bishop known for his uncompromising opposition to Arianism and for being exiled after the Council of Milan in 355. The best-known item under this heading is a short profession of faith, De professione fidei (also called Fides S. Luciferi). It sets out a Nicene creed under Lucifer's name, but he probably did not write it. Its date and origin are uncertain.

Pseudo-Lucius is the name given to writings falsely attributed to Pope Lucius I, bishop of Rome briefly in 253–254. The main piece is a letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal letters compiled in the Frankish kingdom in the mid-ninth century. Other short decrees under his name were passed on through Gratian's twelfth-century Decretum. These texts deal with church discipline and the rights of bishops. They are interesting as evidence for the history of canon law, not for the third-century church.

Pseudo-Macarius is the conventional name for the anonymous author or authors of a Greek ascetic corpus traditionally attributed to Macarius of Egypt. The writings probably date from the late fourth or early fifth century and seem to come from Upper Mesopotamia or Syria. Their best-known part is the Fifty Spiritual Homilies, alongside letters and shorter treatises on prayer, the heart and spiritual perfection. They stress inner struggle against sin and the felt experience of the Holy Spirit. They shaped Eastern Orthodox monasticism and, much later, Pietism and John Wesley.

Pseudo-Marcellinus is the name given to Latin writings falsely attributed to Marcellinus, bishop of Rome from 296 to 304 during Diocletian's persecution. The main pieces are two letters, one to a bishop Salomon and one to the bishops of the East. They belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a ninth-century Frankish collection of forged papal letters. Like the rest of that collection, they use the authority of early popes to support church discipline, the rights of bishops and the primacy of the Roman see.

Pseudo-Marcellus is the name given to the author of Latin letters falsely attributed to Pope Marcellus I, who led the Roman church around 308–309 during and after the Diocletianic persecution. Marcellus left no genuine writings. The letters under his name belong to the forged papal decretals of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, compiled in the Frankish realm in the mid-ninth century. Like the rest of that collection, they use the authority of early popes to support Roman primacy, the rights of bishops and church discipline. They were widely accepted as genuine in medieval canon law.

Pseudo-Mark is the name given to the author or authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Mark, bishop of Rome for a few months in 336. Very little authentic material survives from Mark's short pontificate. Later tradition credited him with letters and decrees, including correspondence with Athanasius of Alexandria. Several of these pieces belong to the forged papal letters of the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, compiled in the ninth century. They are valuable as evidence of how later canon law projected its claims back onto early popes, not as sources for Mark himself.

Pseudo-Maximus of Turin is the conventional name for the anonymous authors of Latin sermons, homilies and letters that were transmitted under the name of Maximus, bishop of Turin, who died in the early fifth century.
