Maximus was a popular preacher, so many later pieces were added to his collection, mostly from northern Italy and later centuries. Early printed editions mixed these pieces with his genuine works. Modern critical scholarship has separated the authentic sermons from the doubtful and spurious ones. The spurious texts are still useful evidence for late antique and early medieval Latin preaching.

Pseudo-Maximus the Confessor is the conventional name for the anonymous authors and compilers of Greek works falsely or doubtfully attributed to Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662). The best known is the Loci communes, a Byzantine florilegium of Christian and pagan sayings arranged in 71 thematic chapters. It was compiled in the late ninth or early tenth century and enlarged around 1000. Another is the Diversa capita ad theologiam et oeconomiam spectantia, a later compilation of ascetic and theological chapters that draws heavily on Maximus's genuine writings. It was handed down under his name.

Pseudo-Melito is the name scholars give to the anonymous authors of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Melito, the second-century bishop of Sardis. These works vary widely in date, language and genre. The Syriac "Discourse in the Presence of Antoninus Caesar" is an apologetic attack on idolatry, and its connection with the Sardian bishop is doubtful. The Clavis Scripturae ("The Key") is a medieval Latin glossary of the allegorical meanings of biblical words. Other works under the name include a Latin Passion of John and a Latin account of Mary's Assumption (Transitus Mariae).

Pseudo-Methodius is the name scholars give to the anonymous authors of writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died in the early fourth century. The Greek corpus includes festal homilies such as the Oration on the Palms and the Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, on the Presentation of Christ in the Temple. These are generally dated later than Methodius himself. The best-known pseudo-Methodian work is a separate text: the late seventh-century Syriac Apocalypse, which was highly influential in medieval apocalyptic thought.

Pseudo-Miltiades is the name given to the author or authors of Latin letters falsely attributed to Miltiades, bishop of Rome from about 311 to 314, the pope under whom the Church gained peace under Constantine. The letters credited to him are generally treated as later forgeries. Most belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal decrees compiled in Francia in the mid-ninth century. The forgeries were meant to give early papal authority to later rules of church discipline and law. Nothing historical is known about who wrote them.

Pseudo-Nonnus, also known as Nonnus Abbas ("Nonnus the Abbot"), was a sixth-century Greek commentator on the orations of Gregory of Nazianzus. Nothing certain is known of his life. His name probably comes from an old misidentification, and he is distinct from the poet Nonnus of Panopolis. His Commentaries, or Mythological Scholia, explain the many allusions to Greek mythology, history and pagan custom in four of Gregory's orations. The work circulated widely in Syriac, Armenian and Georgian translations. The earliest complete text is Paul of Edessa's Syriac version of 623/624, and illustrated manuscripts also survive.

Pseudo-Oecumenius is the name given to the unknown compiler or compilers of Greek New Testament commentaries handed down under the name of Oecumenius. These include commentaries on Acts, the Pauline epistles and the Catholic epistles. They were once credited to a tenth-century bishop of Trikka in Thessaly. Scholars now regard them as separate from the earlier Commentary on the Apocalypse, which is dated to about the sixth or seventh century. The commentaries are largely catena-style compilations of excerpts from earlier Greek fathers. Their exact date and authorship remain uncertain.

Pseudo-Pamphilus is the name for Greek writings attributed, falsely or doubtfully, to Pamphilus of Caesarea, the scholar and martyr who died in 309 and was the teacher of Eusebius. The main work is an Exposition of the Chapters of the Acts of the Apostles, a summary listing the sections of Acts. It belongs to the Euthalian apparatus, a set of prologues, chapter lists and reading aids attached to the Greek text of Acts and the Epistles. Its real author and date are unknown.

Pseudo-Patrick is the conventional name for the authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Saint Patrick, the fifth-century apostle of Ireland. Only his Confessio and Letter to Coroticus are generally accepted as authentic. The attributed works differ in date and origin. One example is De tribus habitaculis, a moral treatise on the three dwellings of heaven, the present world and hell. It circulated under Patrick's name and was also printed among the spurious works of Augustine. Modern scholarship has often credited it to Patrick, bishop of Dublin in the eleventh century.

Pseudo-Paulinus of Nola is the conventional name for the unknown authors of Latin writings that have come down among the works of Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), the Aquitanian-born poet and bishop of Nola, but are considered spurious or doubtful. The best known is a hexameter poem against pagan religion and philosophy, which some manuscripts connect with a certain Antonius. It is usually dated to the late fourth or early fifth century. Its actual author and its exact date remain uncertain.

Pseudo-Peter Chrysologus is the name given to the anonymous Latin authors of sermons that were once attributed to Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna in the fifth century and a noted preacher. His genuine sermons survive chiefly in a collection made by Bishop Felix of Ravenna in the eighth century, but other homilies came to circulate under his name. A group of seven sermons judged not to be his own were handed down separately. Their authors, dates and origins remain uncertain.

Pseudo-Prosper is the name given to Latin works handed down under the name of Prosper of Aquitaine, the fifth-century Gallic theologian and defender of Augustine, whose authorship is false or doubtful. Most come from fifth-century Gaul. The Carmen de providentia divina is a hexameter poem written around 416 in response to the barbarian devastation of Gaul, defending God's providence. The Poema conjugis ad uxorem, also attributed to Paulinus of Nola, is a husband's appeal to his wife to take up a shared ascetic Christian life. A prose Confessio is also ascribed to Prosper, though doubtfully.

Pseudo-Rufinus is the conventional name for the unknown authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 344–412). Rufinus was a monk, historian and translator of Greek theology, especially Origen, so later texts readily gathered under his name. Among them is a short Libellus de fide, or profession of faith, followed by twelve anathemas condemning doctrinal errors. Its real author and date are uncertain. These works do not share a common origin; their only link is the attribution to Rufinus in the manuscripts.

Pseudo-Silvester is the name for Latin writings falsely attributed to Pope Silvester I (314–335). The main text is the Constitutum Silvestri, which presents itself as the canons of a Roman synod held under Silvester. It is generally counted among the "Symmachian forgeries," written in Rome around 501–502 during the dispute between Pope Symmachus and the antipope Laurentius. Its canons on church discipline and clerical rank include the principle that the first see is judged by no one. This idea strongly shaped later medieval teaching on papal immunity from judgement.

Pseudo-Sixtus is the name given to the author or authors of Latin letters and decrees falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Sixtus II. Sixtus was bishop of Rome from 257 to 258 and was martyred with his deacons, including Lawrence, during the persecution under Valerian. No authentic writings of his survive in Latin. The letters circulated under his name are generally regarded as later compositions, and some belong to the forged papal letters of the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. They are valued mainly as evidence for later canon law and the growth of papal tradition.

Pseudo-Sophronius is the name used for Greek writings handed down under the name of Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem (d. 638), but judged spurious or doubtful. The group includes a commentary on the liturgy that explains the rites and symbolism of the Byzantine Eucharist. It is generally thought to be later than Sophronius and to draw on Byzantine liturgical commentary. Other pieces are prayers and an account of the labours, journeys and martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul. The apocryphal narrative of Bartholomew the Apostle's preaching is also linked with this name. Who wrote these texts, and when, remains unknown.

Pseudo-Stephen is the name given to the author of the decretal letters falsely attributed to Pope Stephen I, bishop of Rome from 254 to 257. These letters belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a large collection of forged and altered canon-law texts compiled in the Frankish kingdom around the middle of the ninth century under the name Isidore Mercator. Like the other forged papal letters in the collection, they were written to support papal authority and to protect bishops from accusation and removal. Their forged origin is now universally accepted.

Pseudo-Sulpicius Severus is the name given to the authors of letters that have come down under the name of Sulpicius Severus (c. 363–c. 425), the Aquitanian historian and biographer of Martin of Tours, but whose authenticity is doubtful or rejected. The group includes a collection known as the Seven Letters and other doubtful epistles. Their themes include ascetic life, virginity and moral exhortation. Their actual authors and dates are uncertain, though they are generally placed in the Latin West of late antiquity.

Pseudo-Tertullian is the conventional name for the unknown authors of Latin works once attributed to Tertullian of Carthage and still often printed with his writings. The best known is Against All Heresies, a catalogue of thirty-two heresies, possibly derived from a lost Syntagma of Hippolytus; Victorinus of Pettau has also been suggested as its author. The group also includes several hexameter poems: the Poem against Marcion, sometimes assigned to Commodian, and verse pieces on Genesis, Sodom, Jonah and the Lord's Judgment, some perhaps by Cyprianus Gallus.

Pseudo-Timothy is the conventional name for the unknown author or authors of Coptic writings attributed to an archbishop Timothy of Alexandria. It is unclear which Timothy is meant: Timothy I of the late fourth century and Timothy II Aelurus of the fifth are both possible, and the works probably come from a later period. The best-known text is the Discourse on Abbaton. It tells the story of Abbaton, the angel of death, linking his appointment to the creation and fall of Adam, and reflects the rich angelology of Coptic Christian literature.

Pseudo-Victor of Vita is the name given to anonymous Latin writings that have been transmitted with, or attributed to, Victor of Vita, the late fifth-century North African bishop who chronicled the Vandal persecution of Catholics. The group includes the Passio septem monachorum, an account of seven monks martyred under Vandal rule; the Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae, a list of the African Catholic bishops summoned to the Carthage conference of 484, arranged by province; and a homily on the martyr-bishop Cyprian of Carthage. Their real authorship and dates are uncertain.

Pseudo-Victorinus is the name scholars give to the unknown authors of Latin writings once attributed to Marius Victorinus, the fourth-century Roman rhetorician who converted to Christianity. These pieces were transmitted under his name, but their authorship is now generally rejected or treated as doubtful. The best known is the Liber de physicis, a short theological treatise that probably dates from late antiquity. It deals with creation, the fall and redemption, apparently with an anti-Manichaean purpose. Its real author and exact date remain uncertain.

Pseudo-Zosimus is the name given to the unknown author or authors of Latin writings falsely or doubtfully attributed to Pope Zosimus, bishop of Rome from 417 to 418. Zosimus is remembered for his part in the Pelagian controversy and in disputes over the rights of the churches of Gaul and Africa. Letters were sometimes circulated under the names of early popes to lend them authority in matters of discipline and jurisdiction. Who wrote these letters, and when, is unknown or disputed.

Ptolemy was a Christian Gnostic teacher of the mid-second century and a disciple of Valentinus. He was a leading figure in the western, or Italian, branch of the Valentinian school. He is best known for his Letter to Flora, which survives in full because Epiphanius quoted it in his Panarion. In it he argues that the Mosaic Law came from a just but lesser god rather than from the supreme Father, with parts added by Moses and by the elders. Irenaeus also describes Ptolemy's teachings.

Quadratus (fl. early 2nd century) was a Greek Christian writer and the earliest known Christian apologist. Tradition says he presented a defence of the faith to Emperor Hadrian, probably during the emperor's visit to Athens around 124–125. Only one fragment of this apology survives, preserved by Eusebius. In it Quadratus argues that people whom Jesus healed or raised from the dead were still alive long afterwards, some even into his own time. Later tradition calls him a disciple of the apostles and bishop of Athens, but these identifications are uncertain.

Quintus Julius Hilarianus (fl. 397) was a Latin chronographer and computist from Roman Africa. His writings suggest he was a monk. His identification with the bishop Hilarianus at the Council of Carthage in 411 is uncertain, and he may have been a Donatist. In 397 he wrote the Expositum de die Paschae et mensis, a treatise on Easter, and the Libellus de mundi duratione. The Libellus places the Second Coming in 498, at the world's six-thousandth year, followed by Christ's thousand-year reign. It is one of the last outspoken statements of Latin millenarianism.

Quodvultdeus (died c. 453) was a Latin churchman of Carthage. He was a deacon by 421, corresponded with Augustine of Hippo, and asked him to write De haeresibus. He later became bishop of Carthage. When the Arian Vandal king Gaiseric took the city in 439, he was exiled and sent to Naples, where he died. He is credited with a series of catechetical sermons, including sermons on the Creed for catechumens that were long transmitted under Augustine's name. The Book of the Promises and Predictions of God is also commonly attributed to him.

Rabbula (died 435/436) was bishop of Edessa from 411/412 and one of the leading figures of the early fifth-century Syriac church. Before becoming bishop he was an ascetic, and as bishop he enforced strict discipline over clergy and monks. During the Nestorian controversy that followed the Council of Ephesus (431), he became a firm ally of Cyril of Alexandria and strongly opposed the teachings of Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius. His surviving writings include canons, admonitions to monks, letters, a homily and hymns. He is venerated as a saint in the Syriac Orthodox tradition.

Radegund (c. 520–587) was a Thuringian princess who was taken captive by the Franks in 531 and later married the Merovingian king Chlothar I. She left the marriage, became a deaconess and founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers. The abbey took its name from a relic of the True Cross that she obtained from Byzantium. She was a friend and patron of the poet Venantius Fortunatus. Her Testamentum, a letter to the bishops placing her community under their protection, survives in Gregory of Tours' Histories. She is venerated as a saint.

Reccared I (c. 559–601) was king of the Visigoths from 586 to 601. He ruled Hispania, Gallaecia and Septimania, and was the son and successor of Liuvigild. His reign marked a turning point in the history of Visigothic Spain. In 587 he gave up Arianism for Catholic Christianity, and in 589 the Third Council of Toledo, led by Leander of Seville, formally brought the Gothic nobility and clergy into the Catholic faith. Reccared issued an edict confirming the council's decrees and giving them the force of civil law.

Remigius of Auxerre (c. 841–908) was a Benedictine monk and teacher of the Carolingian period. He studied and taught at the monastery of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, a pupil of Heiric of Auxerre, and later taught at Reims and Paris. He was a teacher of Latin grammar and wrote many commentaries on classical and late antique texts, including works by Martianus Capella, Donatus, Priscian, Boethius and Sedulius's Carmen Paschale. He also compiled the commentaries of earlier medieval scholars, and his teaching passed Carolingian learning on to later generations.

Rhodon was a Greek Christian writer of the late second century. Eusebius reports that he came from Asia and studied under Tatian in Rome. He wrote against the Marcionites and described the divisions among them, including his own conversation with the aged Apelles, Marcion's disciple. Eusebius also mentions a work on Tatian's "Problems" and an intended commentary on the six days of creation. Rhodon's writings are lost apart from fragments, mostly preserved in Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History. They are valuable evidence for second-century Marcionism.

Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 344–411 or 412) was a Latin monk, historian and translator from the region of Aquileia in northern Italy. After living among the monks of Egypt, he founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem with Melania the Elder. He returned to Italy in 397 and translated Greek Christian works into Latin, notably Origen's De Principiis and Eusebius's Church History, which he extended to 395. His defence of Origen led to a bitter quarrel with his former friend Jerome. He also wrote a Commentary on the Apostles' Creed.

Rufinus the Syrian (fl. c. 400) was a Christian priest and theologian, usually counted as a Pelagian. The anti-Pelagian writer Marius Mercator says that a Rufinus "of the Syrian nation" taught at Rome under Pope Anastasius I (399–401) and influenced Pelagius and his followers. Scholars disagree about who he was, and some doubt that he existed at all. He is usually identified as the author of the Liber de fide, which attacks Arianism, Origenism and the doctrine of original sin. That work was long wrongly credited to Rufinus of Aquileia.

Ruricius I (c. 440 – c. 510) was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Limoges around 485 and held the see until his death. Before his ordination he lived as a married layman of high rank. His surviving collection of letters, arranged in two books, is an important source for life in late Roman Gaul under Visigothic rule. The letters show his ties with leading contemporaries such as Sidonius Apollinaris and Faustus of Riez. He is not to be confused with his son-in-law, Rusticus of Lyon.

Flavius Rusticius Helpidius was a Latin Christian poet active in Italy in the late fifth or early sixth century. He is sometimes identified with Helpidius, a deacon and physician at the Ostrogothic court of Theodoric the Great, but the identification is uncertain. Two works are attributed to him. The Carmen de Christi Jesu beneficiis is a hexameter poem praising Christ's saving works and miracles. The Tristicha are a series of three-line poems that pair Old and New Testament scenes typologically, possibly written as captions for paintings.

Rusticus the Deacon was a sixth-century Roman deacon and theologian and a nephew of Pope Vigilius, whom he accompanied to Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy. He opposed Vigilius's concessions to Emperor Justinian, was excommunicated by his uncle around 550, and was later exiled after the Second Council of Constantinople (553). At Constantinople, working in the monastery of the Akoimetoi, he revised Latin translations of the acts of the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon. He also wrote the Contra Acephalos Disputatio, a dialogue defending Chalcedonian Christology against the Miaphysites.

Rusticus the Presbyter was a Latin Christian writer of fifth-century Gaul, active around the 430s and 440s. Very little is known of his life. He is remembered only as the author of a short letter to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, the ascetic writer associated with the monastic circle of Lérins. The letter survives with Eucherius's own writings and shows the learned literary friendships among Gallic clergy and monks of the period. His identification with other men named Rusticus is uncertain.

Salonius was a fifth-century Gallic bishop and Latin ecclesiastical writer. He was a son of Eucherius of Lyon and the brother of Veranus of Vence, and he was educated at Lérins under Hilary of Arles, Salvian and Vincent of Lérins. He became bishop of Geneva around 440 and attended the synods of Orange (441), Vaison (442) and Arles (451). The date of his death is uncertain. He is known for his mystical and allegorical expositions of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. With other Gallic bishops, he also signed a letter to Pope Leo I.

Salvian (Salvianus, c. 400–c. 480) was a Latin Christian writer of fifth-century Roman Gaul. He was probably born in northern Gaul and was married, but he and his wife adopted an ascetic life. He was associated with the monastery of Lérins and later served as a presbyter at Marseilles. His main work, De gubernatione Dei (On the Government of God), argues that the barbarian invasions were God's just judgement on Roman vice, which he contrasts with the virtues of the barbarians. He also wrote Ad ecclesiam, a treatise against avarice, and a number of his letters survive.

Secundinus, known in Irish as Sechnall, was a fifth-century missionary bishop in Ireland. He founded and is patron saint of Domhnach Sechnaill (Dunshaughlin) in County Meath, and is traditionally said to have died around 447–448. Medieval tradition made him a disciple of Saint Patrick and an early bishop of Armagh. Some historians think this link was invented later at Armagh and that he more likely worked alongside Palladius. He is traditionally credited with the Latin alphabetical hymn in praise of Patrick, "Audite omnes amantes Deum," but this attribution is uncertain.

Secundinus was a Manichaean layman, a "hearer" (auditor), who apparently lived in Rome around the start of the fifth century. Not much is known of his life. He is remembered for a Latin letter to Augustine of Hippo, written about 405. In it he praised Augustine's learning and eloquence, criticised his attacks on Manichaeism and urged him to return to the sect. Augustine answered with Contra Secundinum Manichaeum, which he later counted among his best anti-Manichaean writings. The letter is a rare surviving statement of Manichaean views by a Latin follower.

Sedatus of Béziers (Latin Sedatus Biterrensis) was a bishop of Béziers in Septimania, the part of southern Gaul then ruled by the Visigoths. He took part in the Third Council of Toledo in 589, where the Visigothic kingdom formally gave up Arianism for Catholic Christianity. A Latin homily on the Epiphany is attributed to him and is one of very few writings that survive under his name. Little else is known about his life. He should not be confused with Sedatus of Nîmes, who wrote to Ruricius of Limoges around 500.

Sedulius, sometimes given the doubtful nomen Caelius, was a Latin Christian poet of the first half of the fifth century; little is known of his life. His chief work, the Carmen Paschale, is a biblical epic in five books of hexameters on Old Testament wonders and the miracles, death and resurrection of Christ. He also wrote a prose version, the Opus Paschale. Parts of his alphabetic hymn A solis ortus cardine were sung in the Western liturgy at Christmas and Epiphany.

Serapion was bishop of Antioch from about 191 until his death around 211. His writings are lost except for fragments preserved mainly by Eusebius of Caesarea. One is his letter to Caricus and Pontius, written against the Montanist movement. Another comes from his treatise on the Gospel of Peter, addressed to the church at Rhossus. He had first allowed that gospel to be read there, but on examining it he rejected it as containing docetic teaching. This makes him an important early witness to how the churches judged which texts were authentic. His feast is kept on 30 October.

Serapion (or Sarapion) of Thmuis, who died around 362, was an Egyptian monk who became bishop of Thmuis in the Nile Delta in the fourth century. A disciple of Anthony the Great and a close ally of Athanasius of Alexandria, he opposed Arianism. Athanasius addressed his Letters on the Holy Spirit to him. Serapion wrote a treatise against the Manichaeans and several letters. An early Greek euchologion, or bishop's prayer-book, is attributed to him. It contains the earliest recorded use of the Sanctus, though scholars dispute whether he wrote all of it.

Severian (died after 408) was bishop of Gabala in Syria and a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. He won the favour of the Empress Eudoxia. He later became an enemy of John Chrysostom and helped condemn him at the Synod of the Oak. A preacher of the Antiochene school, he left more than fifty sermons on Genesis, Christ, the Holy Spirit, repentance and feasts. Most of the Greek homilies survive under Chrysostom's name. Others are preserved only in Armenian, Coptic, Georgian, Slavonic, Arabic or Latin translation.

Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ was a Coptic Orthodox bishop of al-Ashmunein (Hermopolis Magna) in Upper Egypt. He was active in the later tenth century under the Fatimid caliphate and died in or soon after 987. He complained that Copts no longer understood their own language, and he became one of the first Coptic theologians to write in Arabic. His works include the Book of the Councils (Kitāb al-majāmiʿ). From the eighteenth century he was traditionally named as compiler of the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, but modern scholarship credits that work mainly to Mawhub ibn Mufarrij.

Severus was bishop of Minorca (Menorca) in the Balearic Islands in the early fifth century. He is known solely through his Latin encyclical letter addressed to the whole Church, describing events of early 418 (some date them to 417). He recounts how the arrival of relics of St Stephen heightened tensions with the island's Jewish community, culminating in the burning of the synagogue and the conversion of some 540 Jews within eight days. The letter is a key source for late antique Jewish–Christian relations and the cult of relics.

Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), also called Shenoute the Great or the Archimandrite, was an Egyptian monk and abbot of the White Monastery near Atripe in Upper Egypt. Tradition dates his birth to the mid-fourth century, though his very long reported lifespan has been questioned. He led a large federation of monasteries for men and women and was known for strict discipline and for campaigning against paganism. His Canons and Discourses make him the foremost author of Sahidic Coptic literature. He is among the most venerated saints of the Coptic Orthodox Church.

Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430 – 480s) was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet, diplomat and bishop. He was the son-in-law of Emperor Avitus, and Anthemius made him urban prefect of Rome in 468. In 469 he became Bishop of Clermont. He led the city's resistance to the Visigothic king Euric from 473 to 475, and after its conquest he served as bishop until his death. His Carmina include panegyrics on several emperors. His nine books of letters are a major source for fifth-century Gaul. His writing is dense with classical and biblical allusion. He is venerated as a saint.

Simeon of Beth Arsham (d. c. 548) was a Syriac bishop of Beth Arsham, near Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the Persian Empire. Called the "Persian Debater", he was a leading opponent of the Church of the East and helped build a separate Miaphysite church after the Council of Chalcedon. Most of what is known about his life comes from John of Ephesus's Lives of the Eastern Saints. His best-known work is the Letter on the Himyarite Martyrs, about the massacre of the Christians of Najran. He also wrote a letter against the Nestorians.

Simeon of Mart Maryam was a Syriac Christian writer. He is known only as the author of a letter written in reply to one from a certain Barlaha. His name links him to a place or monastery called Mart Maryam ("Lady Mary"), but nothing certain is known about his life, his dates or his church office. The surviving exchange of letters is his only known contribution to Syriac literature.

Sisebut (c. 565–621) was King of the Visigoths in Hispania, Gallaecia and Septimania from 612 until his death. He campaigned against the Byzantine possessions in southern Spain and is remembered for anti-Jewish measures, including forced baptisms. He was a patron and correspondent of Isidore of Seville, who dedicated his De natura rerum to him, and was an unusually learned ruler. His Latin writings include letters, a Life and Passion of Desiderius of Vienne, and a poem on eclipses addressed to Isidore.

Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439), was a Greek Christian church historian who lived and worked in Constantinople. He was a layman, possibly a lawyer, and wrote at the same time as Sozomen and Theodoret. His Ecclesiastical History, in seven books, continues Eusebius of Caesarea's history and covers the years 305 to 439. It deals with the Arian controversy, the councils, and the emperors of the period. Historians value it for its fairly balanced judgements and for quoting documents directly.

Sonnatius was bishop of Reims in Merovingian Gaul in the early seventh century. He held the see from about 613 until his death in 631. He is known as the author of a short set of Statuta, disciplinary regulations for the clergy and faithful of his diocese. They are among the earliest surviving episcopal statutes from the Frankish church, and the tenth-century historian Flodoard preserved them in his history of the church of Reims. Sonnatius also took part in the Frankish church councils of his time.

Sophronius (c. 560–638), sometimes called "the Sophist", was a Greek monk, theologian and poet who served as Patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 until his death. He was born in Damascus and travelled widely with John Moschus. He was the leading early opponent of monoenergism and monothelitism, and set out his position in a synodical letter. In 637 or 638 he surrendered Jerusalem to Caliph Umar. His writings include homilies, the Anacreontic poems, and an account of the miracles of Saints Cyrus and John. The Life of Mary of Egypt is traditionally attributed to him.

Salamanes Hermias Sozomenos, known as Sozomen (c. 400 – c. 450), was a lawyer and church historian. He came from Bethelia near Gaza in Palestine and practised law in Constantinople. His Ecclesiastical History, in nine books dedicated to Emperor Theodosius II, carries on Eusebius's account of the church from about 324 into the reign of Theodosius II. The work leans heavily on the history of Socrates Scholasticus, but Sozomen adds material of his own, especially on monasticism, Palestine, and Christianity among the Persians and Goths.

Stepane Mtbevari (Stephen of Tbeti) was a tenth-century Georgian churchman, writer and calligrapher. He became the first bishop of Tbeti in Shavsheti, a see founded by the Bagratid prince Ashot Kukhi of Tao (d. 918). Ashot also commissioned his best-known surviving work, the Martyrdom (Passion) of Gobron. It tells how the Georgian noble Gobron defended the fortress of Q'ueli and was put to death in 914 by the Sajid emir Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj. Besides this original hagiography, Stepane translated a commentary on the Psalms. Giorgi Merchule praised him as a writer.

Stephen was a Latin abbot in late sixth-century Gaul, known only as a correspondent of Aunarius (Aunacharius), bishop of Auxerre from about 572 to 605. His surviving letter to Aunarius belongs to the literary activity the bishop sponsored around the cults of the saints of Auxerre. He is often identified with the Stephen, sometimes called "the African", who wrote hagiographical works at Aunarius's request, but the identification is uncertain. Almost nothing else is known of his life, monastery or dates.

Stephen was an abbot who, together with a certain Paul, is named as joint author of the Regula Pauli et Stephani, a short Latin monastic rule addressed to monks. Almost nothing is known of his life. The rule is usually dated to the sixth century, but where it was written is disputed, with Italy and Spain both proposed. It deals mainly with the practical discipline of community life, including the divine office, work, silence and obedience, and belongs to the body of early Western monastic rules from before Benedict's rule became dominant.

Stephen of Hnes was a Coptic bishop of Hnes (Greek Heracleopolis Magna, modern Ahnas) in Middle Egypt. He probably lived in the sixth century or somewhat later, but his exact dates are uncertain. He is known for his hagiographical encomia in Sahidic Coptic. One is a panegyric on Apollo, archimandrite of the monastery of Isaac, a leader of anti-Chalcedonian monasticism. The other is an encomium on the martyr Helias. These texts are valuable evidence for Egyptian monastic life and for the cult of the saints in the post-Chalcedonian Coptic church.

Stephen the Deacon was a Byzantine cleric, traditionally identified as a deacon of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, who was active in the early ninth century. He is known only as the author of the Life of Stephen the Younger, written around 806–809. Its subject was a monk of Mount Auxentius who was put to death in 765 under Emperor Constantine V for opposing iconoclasm. The work is a major iconophile hagiography and an important source for the first period of Byzantine iconoclasm.

Sulpicius II, called the Pious (died 17 January 646 or 647), was a Merovingian bishop of Bourges and is venerated as a saint. Before entering the episcopate he served at the Frankish royal court. He became bishop around 624, succeeding Austregisilus, and was remembered for his asceticism, his charity to the poor, and his pastoral care. He should not be confused with his predecessor Sulpicius I, called the Severe. A small collection of three Latin letters survives under his name, and these belong to the Gallic correspondence of his time.

Sulpicius Severus (c. 363 – c. 425) was a Latin Christian writer and historian from Aquitania in Gaul. He was trained in law and came from a noble family. After his wife died he took up an ascetic life under the influence of Martin of Tours, whom he knew personally. His Life of Saint Martin became a founding model of Western hagiography, and he added to it in letters and in the Dialogues. He also wrote the Chronica, a concise history of the world from the Creation to about 400 AD.

Sumbat Davitis-dze, "Sumbat son of David", was an eleventh-century Georgian chronicler. He wrote The Life and Tale of the Bagratids, a history of the Bagrationi royal dynasty of Georgia from its origins to about 1030. The scholar Ekvtime Takaishvili argued that Sumbat himself belonged to the dynasty. His chronicle is the earliest major written statement of the Bagratid claim to descend from the biblical King David. This claim became central to the dynasty's royal ideology, although modern scholarship rejects it.

Symeon Metaphrastes (died c. 1000) was a Byzantine writer and high court official in Constantinople. The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint, with a feast on 9 or 28 November. He is best known for his ten-volume Greek menologion, a collection of saints' lives arranged by the church calendar. In it he reworked older hagiographical texts into a more polished literary style, and this "metaphrasis" earned him his epithet. Other works attributed to him include moral discourses excerpted from Basil of Caesarea. Whether he was the same person as the chronicler Symeon Logothete is uncertain.

Symeon Stylites the Younger (521–596/597), also called Symeon of the Wondrous (Admirable) Mountain, was a Christian ascetic from Antioch. Following the model of Symeon Stylites the Elder, he lived on pillars from childhood, eventually settling on the Wondrous Mountain near Antioch. There he became famous as a wonderworker, counsellor and spiritual guide. Writings attributed to him include ascetic sermons, a letter to Emperor Justin II, and a passage on holy images later cited by iconophiles, though its authenticity has been questioned. He is venerated as a saint in both East and West.

Symeon the New Theologian (c. 949–1022) was a Byzantine monk, mystic and poet. Born into the nobility, he became a disciple of Symeon the Studite in Constantinople. He served for about twenty-five years as abbot of the Monastery of Saint Mamas, but conflict with church authorities ended in his exile. He taught that believers can directly experience God, often described as divine light. His works include the Catechetical Discourses, the Hymns of Divine Love, and practical and theological chapters, some of which were later included in the Philokalia.

Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 345–402) was a Roman senator, orator and statesman. He governed proconsular Africa in 373, served as urban prefect of Rome in 384–385 and was consul in 391. As a leading defender of Rome's traditional religion, he is best known for his third Relatio of 384. In it he asked Emperor Valentinian II to restore the Altar of Victory to the Senate house, and Ambrose of Milan wrote a reply rejecting the request. His large collection of letters and his official dispatches survive, along with fragments of his speeches.

Symphosius, sometimes less properly called Symposius, was a Latin poet of late antiquity, probably active in the fourth or fifth century. Almost nothing is known of his life. Some scholars have suggested he came from North Africa, but this is uncertain. He wrote the Aenigmata, a collection of one hundred riddles, each in three hexameter lines, and they have come down to us with their solutions. A verse preface sets the collection at the festival of the Saturnalia. The riddles strongly influenced early medieval riddle-writers, notably Aldhelm and other Anglo-Latin poets.

Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373 – c. 414) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher, orator and poet from a wealthy family of Cyrenaica. He studied in Alexandria under Hypatia and went on an embassy to Constantinople, where he delivered his speech De regno before the emperor Arcadius. Around 410 he became bishop of Ptolemais while keeping many of his philosophical views. His writings include Dion, the Praise of Baldness, On Providence, On Dreams, a treatise on the astrolabe, many letters and hymns combining Christian and Neoplatonic thought.

Taio (also Tajo; c. 600–c. 683) was a Visigothic theologian and bishop of Zaragoza. He succeeded his teacher Braulio in 651. Before becoming bishop he travelled to Rome to find copies of the works of Gregory the Great. A later account of a vision embellished this journey, saying the vision showed him where the manuscripts lay. His main work is the Sententiarum libri quinque, which he began around 653 at the request of Bishop Quiricus of Barcelona. It arranges extracts, mainly from Gregory, into a systematic survey of doctrine and Christian life. Some of his letters also survive.

Tarasius (c. 730–806) was Patriarch of Constantinople from 784 until his death. A layman and senior imperial secretary under Empress Irene, he was raised directly to the patriarchate. He presided over the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which condemned iconoclasm and restored the veneration of icons. His later tolerance of Emperor Constantine VI's second marriage provoked the Moechian controversy and criticism from strict monastics such as Theodore the Studite. His surviving writings include letters and an encomiastic oration. He is venerated as a saint.

Tarra was a monk in Visigothic Spain in the late sixth century, during the reign of King Reccared (586–601). Almost nothing is known of him apart from a single surviving letter to the king. In it he protests that he was unjustly expelled from his monastery on charges of misconduct, and he appeals to Reccared for redress. The letter survives in the collection known as the Epistolae Wisigothicae. It offers rare evidence of monastic discipline and of how the Catholic Visigothic monarchy was approached soon after its conversion.

Tatian (c. 120–c. 180), called "the Assyrian", was a second-century Christian apologist and ascetic. He was born in the East, possibly in Adiabene. He became a Christian in Rome and studied under Justin Martyr. After Justin's death he returned to the East, and Irenaeus links him with the rigorist Encratites. His Address to the Greeks is a sharp attack on Greek culture and philosophy. His most influential work, the Diatessaron, wove the four gospels into one narrative. It served as the standard gospel text in Syriac-speaking churches until the fifth century.

Tertullian (Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus, c. 155 – after c. 220) was an early Christian writer from Carthage in Roman Africa. He was the first author to produce a large body of Christian literature in Latin, and he is often called the father of Latin Christianity. He was an apologist, writing Apology and Ad Nationes, and a polemicist against heresy, writing Against Marcion, Against Praxeas and Against the Valentinians. He is the earliest Latin writer known to use the term trinitas. In later life he was drawn to Montanism.

Thalassius the Libyan, or Thalassius the Abbot, was a Greek monastic writer of the seventh century and head of a monastery in the Libyan desert. He was a friend and correspondent of Maximus the Confessor, who addressed his long work of scriptural exegesis, the Questions to Thalassius, to him. Thalassius is known for four "centuries" of short ascetic sayings, On Love, Self-Control and Life in Accordance with the Intellect. They draw on the teaching of Maximus and Evagrius and were later included in the Philokalia.

Theodore Abu Qurrah (c. 750 – c. 825) was a Melkite bishop and theologian. He was probably born in Edessa and served as bishop of Harran in the early Islamic period. He was one of the first Christian theologians to write extensively in Arabic, and he also wrote in Syriac. A collection of short Greek treatises, or opuscula, is also attributed to him. In these works he defended Chalcedonian Christology against Jacobites and Nestorians, argued against Muslims and Jews, and defended the veneration of icons. He is a key figure in early Arabic Christian apologetic.

Theodore Lector (Theodoros Anagnostes) was a reader at the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in the early sixth century. He wrote two works of church history. The first, the Tripartite History, compiled extracts from the historians Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, and covers the years from Constantine's early reign in 313 to 439. The second, his own Ecclesiastical History, continued the story from the death of Theodosius II in 450 to the accession of Justin I in 518. It survives only in fragments and excerpts, but it is valuable because little other evidence exists for that period.

Theodore of Heraclea (died c. 355) was a Greek bishop and biblical commentator. He became bishop of Heraclea (Perinthus) in Thrace between 328 and 334, and was a prominent ally of Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party against Athanasius. The Western bishops at Serdica condemned him, and he was later deposed. Jerome says he wrote commentaries on Matthew, John, the Pauline epistles and the Psalms during the reign of Constantius II. Only fragments of his exegesis survive, mostly in catenae, including comments on Isaiah. His interpretation emphasizes the literal and historical sense.

Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428) was a Greek theologian and biblical exegete. He was born at Antioch and served as a presbyter there before becoming bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia in 392. As the leading figure of the Antiochene school, he favoured literal and historical interpretation of Scripture. He wrote many commentaries, including one on the Twelve Minor Prophets, as well as catechetical homilies. The Council of Constantinople condemned him posthumously in 553, so much of his work survives only in fragments, Latin versions and Syriac translations. The Church of the East honours him as "the Interpreter".

Theodore of Raithu was a Greek Christian theologian and monk at Raithu on the Sinai Peninsula. He was active after 550, in the late sixth or early seventh century, and is often counted as the last of the Neo-Chalcedonians. Some scholars identify him with Theodore, bishop of nearby Pharan, an early monenergist who died before 625. His main work, the Preparation (Proparaskeue), tries to reconcile Cyril of Alexandria's terminology with Chalcedon. In it he refutes christological heresies from Mani to Severus and then sets out Chalcedonian Christology in philosophical terms. The treatise De sectis is sometimes also attributed to him.

Theodore of Scythopolis was a sixth-century Greek churchman who became bishop of Scythopolis (modern Beth Shean), the metropolitan see of Palestina Secunda, around the time of the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. He was linked with the Origenist controversies that divided the Palestinian monasteries under Justinian. He is known for a short treatise, the Libellus de erroribus Origenis, which condemns Origenist doctrines in a series of anathemas. Few details of his life are securely known.

Theodore of Tabennese (c. 314–368), also called Abba Theodore or Theodore the Sanctified, was an Egyptian monk in Upper Egypt. He joined Pachomius as a young man and became his closest disciple and spiritual successor in the Pachomian community. After the founder's death, a crisis threatened the first federation of cenobitic monasteries. Theodore, working alongside the abbot Horsiesius, held the federation together and directed it until his death. Monastic instructions and letters are attributed to him, and his life is recorded in the Pachomian Lives.

Theodore the Studite (759–826) was a Byzantine monk and abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. He led a revival of Byzantine monastic life. His reforms stressed community life, manual labour and strict discipline, and his rule became a model for later monasteries, including those of Mount Athos and Kievan Rus'. He strongly opposed iconoclasm and also clashed with emperors and patriarchs over other issues, so he was exiled several times. His writings include catecheses addressed to his monks, a large body of letters, hymns, and treatises defending the veneration of icons.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393 – c. 458/466) was a Greek theologian of the Antiochene school and bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria from 423. He was a leading biblical commentator and wrote works including an Ecclesiastical History continuing Eusebius, the Religious History about Syrian ascetics, and commentaries on the Song of Songs, Daniel and Ezekiel. In the Christological controversies he opposed Cyril of Alexandria's Twelve Anathemas and condemned Nestorius only at the Council of Chalcedon (451). Some of his writings against Cyril were condemned after his death in 553, during the Three Chapters controversy.

Theodoric the Great (c. 454–526) was king of the Ostrogoths and, from 493, ruler of Italy, governing from Ravenna. As a boy he was held hostage in Constantinople, where he received a Roman education. At Emperor Zeno's urging he overthrew Odoacer, then kept Roman law and administration in place and backed a major building programme. Although he was a Homoian (Arian) Christian, he stepped into the disputed papal election between Symmachus and Laurentius. His written orders (praeceptiones) to the Roman synods of 501 that dealt with the schism survive.

Theodosius I (347–395), called Theodosius the Great, was Roman emperor from 379 to 395. Born in Hispania, he was the son of the general Theodosius the Elder. Gratian made him emperor after Valens died at Adrianople. He ended the Gothic War in 382 by settling the Goths inside the empire, and he was the last emperor to rule both East and West. His religious legislation, including the edict of Thessalonica (380), and the Council of Constantinople (381) made Nicene Christianity the orthodox faith of the empire. Many of his decrees survive in the Theodosian Code.

Theodosius I (died 566) was Patriarch of Alexandria from 535. He was the last patriarch recognised by both the Miaphysite (later Coptic) and Chalcedonian communities. Installed with imperial support after the brief tenure of Gaianus, he was deposed and exiled by Justinian in 536 for his Miaphysite theology. He spent much of his remaining life in Constantinople, where he led the exiled anti-Chalcedonians under Empress Theodora's protection and consecrated Jacob Baradaeus. His writings include a Tome to Theodora, letters, and homilies preserved in Coptic.

Theodosius was a sixth-century Latin writer and pilgrim, known only as the author of De situ terrae sanctae, a short account of the Holy Land. A ninth-century manuscript calls him a German archdeacon, but nothing else is known about his life. His work was written between about 518 and 530. It lists holy places, routes and distances, and sometimes comments on related biblical passages. It mixes the form of a pilgrim itinerary with stories closer to a travel narrative.

Theodotus of Ancyra was a Greek theologian and bishop of Ancyra (modern Ankara) in the fifth century. He was at first close to Nestorius of Constantinople. At the Council of Ephesus in 431, however, he sided with Cyril of Alexandria in condemning him, and the Nestorian party condemned Theodotus in turn at the Synod of Tarsus in 432. His surviving writings belong to the Christological controversy. They include homilies, among them sermons on the Nativity, an exposition of the Nicene Creed and letters. He probably died before about 446.

Theognostus of Alexandria was a Christian theologian of the later third century. He is thought to have been a follower of Origen, and Philip of Side says he led the catechetical school of Alexandria. Eusebius and Jerome do not mention him. His main work, the Hypotyposes ("Outlines") in seven books, was a systematic treatment of Christian doctrine. Photius summarized it and criticized some of its Origenist views. Only fragments survive, including passages quoted by Athanasius on the Son's relation to the Father.

Theognostus the Monk was a Byzantine monk active in the mid-ninth century. He was a supporter of Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, who was deposed in 858 and replaced by Photius. Theognostus went to Rome and appealed to Pope Nicholas I for Ignatius. He is known for a petition (libellus) addressed to the pope in Ignatius's name. It gives the Ignatian party's account of the deposition and asks for papal intervention, and it is an important document for the early phase of the Photian controversy between Rome and Constantinople.

Theophanes the Confessor (c. 759–817 or 818), also called Theophanes of the Great Field, was a Byzantine aristocrat who served at the court of Emperor Leo IV before becoming a monk. He attended the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. Later he opposed the iconoclasm of Leo V the Armenian and was imprisoned for it. He died soon after his release. His Chronographia is an annalistic chronicle of the years 285 to 813. It is a major source for Byzantine history and for the early Islamic conquests. He is venerated as a saint on 12 March.

Theophilus of Alexandria (died 412) was patriarch of Alexandria from 385 until his death and the uncle and predecessor of Cyril of Alexandria. He acted forcefully against paganism, most famously in the destruction of the Serapeum in 391. He also turned against Origenism, expelling the Origenist monks of Nitria, and at the Synod of the Oak in 403 he brought about the deposition of John Chrysostom. Most of his writings survive only in part. They include festal letters, some preserved in Jerome's Latin translation, and short canonical rulings that were taken into the Greek collections of church law.

Theophilus of Antioch was a Greek Christian apologist and bishop of Antioch from about 169 until his death, probably between 183 and 185. He was born a pagan near the Tigris and Euphrates and became a Christian through reading the Scriptures, especially the prophets. His only surviving work is To Autolycus, a defence of Christianity in three books addressed to a pagan friend. It is the earliest Christian text known to use the term "Triad" (trias) for God. Eusebius records that he also wrote a work against Marcion, which is now lost.

Theophilus (died c. 196) was bishop of Caesarea Maritima in Palestine in the late second century. According to Eusebius, he presided with Narcissus of Jerusalem over a synod held in Palestine during the Paschal controversy under Pope Victor of Rome. The synod supported celebrating Easter on Sunday against the Quartodeciman practice. Eusebius preserves a fragment of its synodal letter, which mentions the churches of Palestine and Alexandria keeping Easter on the same day. Later traditions about him are less reliable. He is commemorated as a saint on 5 March.

Theotimus of Tomi, sometimes called Theotimus II to distinguish him from the earlier bishop of the same see who was a friend of John Chrysostom, was bishop of Tomi in Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast in the mid-fifth century. He is known almost entirely from his letter to Emperor Leo I, written around 458. The letter was a reply to the emperor's inquiry to the bishops about the authority of the Council of Chalcedon and the disputed situation of the church of Alexandria. Little else is known of his life.

Thomas of Edessa (Tōmā ūrhāyā, died c. 540) was a Syriac theologian of the Church of the East. He was educated at Edessa, where he taught Greek to the future patriarch Aba. He later travelled with Aba through the Roman Empire, including to Constantinople, and studied and taught at the school of Nisibis. His theology followed Theodore of Mopsuestia. Most of his writings are lost. His explanations of the feasts of the Nativity and Epiphany are the oldest surviving examples of the Syriac ʿeltā, or "cause", genre. Cyrus of Edessa later continued this work.

Timothy I was bishop of Alexandria from 381 until his death in 384 or 385. He succeeded his brother Peter II in the see. In the Coptic tradition he is counted as the twenty-second patriarch of Alexandria. He took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. He is chiefly remembered for his Canonical Answers (Responsa canonica), short replies to questions on church discipline that cover baptism, the Eucharist, penance and ritual purity. These answers were taken into the Greek collections of canon law and gained lasting authority in Byzantine and later Orthodox church practice.

Timothy I (died 5 April 518) was Patriarch of Constantinople from 511 to 518. Before that he was a priest of the city. Emperor Anastasius I appointed him after deposing Patriarch Macedonius II. Timothy supported the emperor's religious policy, which favoured opponents of the Council of Chalcedon, and this made him a controversial figure among Chalcedonian Christians. He is traditionally credited with a Greek treatise, De iis qui ad Ecclesiam accedunt. It sorts heretics into classes according to how each should be received into the Church. Many scholars assign this work to a later Timothy, a presbyter of Constantinople.

Timothy was the anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) Patriarch of Alexandria from 517 until his death on 7 February 535. Byzantine historians usually number him Timothy IV. The Coptic Orthodox Church counts him as Timothy III, its 32nd pope, because it does not recognise the Chalcedonian Timothy Salophakiolos. During his patriarchate Alexandria sheltered opponents of the Council of Chalcedon who had been driven from Syria, among them Severus of Antioch. Some of his theological writings and sermons survive, mostly in fragments. His successor was Theodosius I.

Timothy of Berytus (Timotheus Berytensis) was a Greek-speaking churchman of the later fourth century. He was a leading disciple of Apollinaris of Laodicea and the Apollinarian bishop of Berytus, modern Beirut. He defended Apollinaris's teaching that in Christ the divine Logos took the place of a human rational mind, a view condemned by the wider Church. His writings survive only in fragments, mostly letters quoted by later authors, and these are a valuable source for Apollinarian Christology in the generation after its founder.

Timothy of Jerusalem was a Greek Christian preacher, traditionally described as a presbyter of Jerusalem. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his dates are uncertain: he is usually placed somewhere between the fifth and seventh centuries. A small number of homilies circulate under his name, chiefly on feasts connected with the life of Christ, such as the Presentation in the Temple and the meeting with Simeon. Scholars continue to debate whether these attributions are authentic.

Titus of Bostra (died c. 378) was a Greek-speaking theologian and bishop of Bostra, capital of the Roman province of Arabia. Under Julian the Apostate he clashed with the emperor, who in 362 wrote to the people of Bostra urging them to expel him. He is best known for Against the Manichaeans, a refutation in four books that defends the goodness of creation and God's providence. The Greek original survives only in part, but a complete early Syriac translation exists. Fragments of his homilies on Luke also survive.

Trifolius was a Latin presbyter and theologian of the early sixth century, probably active in Rome. Little is known of his life. He is remembered for a letter of 519/520 to the Roman senator Faustus against John, one of the Scythian monks. In it he rejected their Theopaschite formula, "One of the Trinity suffered," and argued that it appeared in none of the four ecumenical councils and had in effect already been condemned at Chalcedon. He also likened the monks' views to those of the Arians and Apollinarians.

Troianus (Latin Troianus Santonensis) was bishop of Saintes in western Gaul in the early sixth century. He was active from about 511 and died around 532. Little is known of his life, and he was later venerated locally as a saint. One Latin letter by him survives, addressed to Eumerius, bishop of Nantes. It answers a pastoral question about the sacraments, generally understood to be whether people whose baptism was uncertain should be baptized. The letter is a small piece of evidence for church discipline in Merovingian Gaul.

Ticonius (also Tyconius), active c. 370–390, was a Latin Christian theologian of North Africa and a lay member of the Donatist church. His view of the Church as a mixed body of good and wicked led to his condemnation by a Donatist council around 380, though he never joined the Catholics. His Book of Rules (De septem regulis), the first Latin handbook of biblical interpretation, was adopted by Augustine in On Christian Doctrine. His lost Commentary on the Apocalypse shaped later exegesis, including that of Beatus of Liébana.

Uranius was a Latin presbyter of the early fifth century and a member of the clergy around Paulinus, bishop of Nola in Campania. He is known only from his letter De obitu sancti Paulini, addressed to a certain Pacatus. It gives an eyewitness account of the last days and death of Paulinus in 431, presenting him as a model of saintly charity and humility. The letter is an important source for Paulinus's final years and an early example of hagiographical writing about him.

Ursacius was bishop of Singidunum (modern Belgrade) in the mid-fourth century and a leading figure in the Arian controversy. He usually acted alongside Valens of Mursa and later Germinius of Sirmium. He opposed Athanasius at the Council of Tyre in 335 and was condemned at Serdica in 343. Around 347 he and Valens recanted in a letter to Pope Julius I and accepted Athanasius. They later went back to an anti-Nicene, Homoian position and promoted the creeds of Sirmium and the settlement reached at Rimini in 359.

Valens of Mursa was a fourth-century bishop of Mursa (modern Osijek, Croatia) and a leading opponent of the Nicene party, often named together with Ursacius of Singidunum. He took part in the Council of Tyre (335), which condemned Athanasius. Around 347 he wrote a letter to Pope Julius I renouncing his earlier position, but he later went back to it. He had influence with Emperor Constantius II and helped shape the Homoian creeds of Sirmium and the Council of Ariminum (359). His opponents commonly called him an Arian.

Valentinian II (371–392) was Roman emperor in the West from 375 to 392. The son of Valentinian I and Justina, he was proclaimed emperor at the age of four and ruled at first as junior colleague of his half-brother Gratian. His court at Milan was the scene of conflict between Nicene and Arian Christians, notably involving Ambrose. He fled from the usurper Magnus Maximus in 387, was restored by Theodosius I, and later ruled from Gaul under the general Arbogast. He was found dead in 392. Official imperial letters survive in his name.

Valentinus was abbot of a monastery at Hadrumetum (modern Sousse, Tunisia) in Roman North Africa in the early fifth century. Around 426–427 his community was troubled by disputes over grace and free will, prompted by Augustine's letter to Sixtus. Some monks feared that Augustine's teaching made human effort and correction pointless. Augustine replied with De gratia et libero arbitrio and De correptione et gratia. Valentinus's letter to Augustine survives among Augustine's correspondence. It explains the controversy and thanks him for his guidance, and it is an important witness to the early stages of the Semi-Pelagian debate.
